When implementation begins, the code's named layout constants trace directly back to the approved spec, and EditMode tests assert the built UI's actual anchors/margins/sizes against them.

This is what lets Derek and Lucas approve a design without loading the game: structural correctness is test-verified against the spec's constants, so only final art/color/font polish still wants a glance at a real build.

docs.title: The loop
docs.text:
propose ──▶ review ──▶ approve ──▶ distill ──▶ implement ──▶ verify
(dual      (Derek/    (recorded   (into        (against     (EditMode
 artifact)  Lucas)     on issue)   docs/specs/  named        tests vs.
                                   ui/)         constants)   constants)
  1. Propose. On the wireframe's GitHub issue, produce the dual artifact: the structured text-spec page and the corresponding HTML mockup. Nothing about the screen's style gets re-decided here — that's Art & UI Style's job; the proposal composes already-decided style into a layout.
  2. Review. Derek and Lucas review the proposal — reading the text spec and opening the HTML mockup. Feedback loops back into the proposal until it's right.
  3. Approve. Approval is recorded on the wireframe issue (a comment or a checked box), the same lightweight record used elsewhere. Approval is of the layout, its regions, and its named constants.
  4. Distill. The approved wireframe lands in docs/specs/ui/ as the screen's page plus its mockup — this is now the authoritative layout contract for that screen, just like any other specs page.
  5. Implement. Implementation code declares the spec's named constants (per #161) and builds the layout against them — test-first, per Testing Strategy.
  6. Verify. EditMode tests assert the built UI's actual anchors, margins, and sizes match the named constants. CI is the authoritative green (EditMode tests run in CI).

docs.title: The gate
docs.text:
If an issue would touch a screen's structure (adding, removing, or repositioning regions of a panel/overlay/screen) and no approved wireframe exists for it, stop and flag it — do not implement, not even graybox. This has the same posture as the docs-conflict rule: it's a design gap to resolve back in GitHub (file/finish the wireframe first), not something to invent mid-implementation.

Purely visual restyling that doesn't move structure (e.g. applying an already-approved shared-component style) is not gated by this rule — but if you're unsure whether a change is structural, treat it as structural and flag it.

docs.title: How a wireframe issue is recognized: the type:wireframe label
docs.text:
A GitHub issue whose deliverable is the wireframe itself (the dual artifact of step 1) carries the type:wireframe label, alongside a Wireframe: title prefix (existing practice, e.g. #374). The label is the authoritative marker; the title prefix is a human-readable convention.

This matters to the pipeline's blocker auto-revisit sweep. A downstream issue Blocked by: a wireframe issue is hard-gated on the wireframe reaching approve → distill → closed, not merely on it entering the dev queue — so the sweep treats a type:wireframe blocker as resolved only once it is closed, never at ready-for-work/in-progress (#396). An ordinary blocker still resolves as soon as it is queued. Apply type:wireframe when filing a wireframe issue so the sweep gates its dependents correctly.

docs.title: Hand-Authoring Unity Serialized Assets
docs.text: Development agents work in sandboxes without a Unity Editor, so .meta files and ProjectSettings.asset edits are written by hand as YAML. Unity's serialization has several silent failure modes that cost real debugging rounds when the app icon and splash screen were wired up (PRs #132, #133). This page is the accumulated field guide — read it before hand-authoring any Unity YAML.

docs.title: The golden rule: never guess — verify against real project files
docs.text:
Unity ignores serialized entries it doesn't understand silently, at build time. There is no error, no warning, no failing import — the feature just doesn't exist in the build. Guessed key names and enum values are therefore worse than compile errors: they ship.

Before writing a block you haven't written before, find real-world ProjectSettings.asset / .meta examples in public repos (web search for the key name) and copy the exact key names, value shapes, sibling keys, and ordering.

Case study: the Android adaptive icon was first serialized with a guessed m_Kind: 5. Unity ignored the entry and shipped the raw square legacy icon. Real files revealed the actual enum: Legacy = 0, Round = 1, Adaptive = 2 — and that Unity expects all six density entries (432/324/216/162/108/81), not one.

docs.title: 1. GUID references require committed .meta files
docs.text:
The repo convention for art models (FBX/PNG under Assets/Art/) is to not commit .meta files for binaries — Unity generates them locally and nothing depends on the GUID.

That convention inverts the moment anything references the asset by GUID (ProjectSettings.asset, a scene, another asset): the .meta must be hand-authored with a pinned GUID and committed, or every machine generates a different GUID and the reference breaks. Current pinned-GUID assets: the app icon, its adaptive layers, and the splash cover art (all under Assets/Art/Icon/ and Assets/Art/Splash/).

docs.title: 2. Sprite references use fileID: 21300000 — and sprite IDs must be pinned
docs.text:
A texture asset exposes different sub-assets with different fileIDs:

Reference fileID Texture2D (e.g. app icons) 2800000 Sprite sub-asset (e.g. splash backgrounds) 21300000

PlayerSettings.SplashScreen.background is typed Sprite, so the splash background must reference {fileID: 21300000, guid: ..., type: 3} and the PNG's importer must produce a Sprite (textureType: 8, spriteMode: 1).

The trap inside the trap: modern Unity randomizes sprite internal IDs on fresh import. A hand-authored reference to 21300000 only survives a from-scratch Library rebuild (i.e. CI, or any fresh clone) if the .meta pins the ID via internalIDToNameTable:

  internalIDToNameTable:
  - first:
      213: 21300000
    second: cover-art

See Assets/Art/Splash/cover-art.png.meta for the working example.

docs.title: 3. Some settings persist in editor-source AND runtime field pairs — set both
docs.text:
Unity sometimes stores the same value twice: an editor-facing "source" field and the field the built player actually reads, with the Editor UI copying source → runtime when you assign it. Hand-authoring only the source half produces a build where the feature silently falls back to its default.

Case study: the splash background. splashScreenBackgroundSourceLandscape/Portrait are the editor source slots; m_SplashScreenBackgroundLandscape/Portrait are the runtime-facing pair. Setting only the source pair shipped a splash that showed just the solid background color.

If a real-world file shows the same reference under two key names, that's this pattern — author both.

Honest status: authoring both pairs was verified correct at the Editor level (Player Settings UI showed the sprite in both slots; the splash Preview rendered it), but the Android CI build still rendered only the background color — the residual failure sits in the build stage, not serialization, and the feature was parked. Full evidence and resume instructions: #136.

docs.title: 4. EditMode tests must assert serialization, not PlayerSettings object references
docs.text:
PlayerSettings deserializes once at editor startup. On a fresh Library rebuild (every CI run), assets referenced by nothing in a scene are imported lazily, after startup — so PlayerSettings.GetIconsForTargetGroup(...) style APIs return null texture references for the whole session even when the serialized wiring is correct. A test asserting those references passes locally (warm Library) and fails on CI, or worse, can't ever pass on CI.

Instead:

  • Assert on the YAML text of ProjectSettings.asset (regex the block, check pinned GUIDs and exact enum values — pin values like m_Kind: 2 so a bad edit can't ship silently).
  • Assert asset existence with AssetDatabase.ImportAsset(path, ImportAssetOptions.ForceSynchronousImport) followed by LoadAssetAtPath — never rely on something else having imported it first.
  • For pinned sub-asset IDs, AssetDatabase.TryGetGUIDAndLocalFileIdentifier verifies both GUID and fileID.

Assets/Tests/EditMode/AppIconTests.cs and SplashScreenTests.cs are the reference implementations.

docs.title: 5. Runtime-built UGUI needs its shader in Always-Included and a bundled font
docs.text:
UGUI built procedurally at runtime (gameObject.AddComponent<Image>() / <Text>(), no serialized scene/prefab) is a serialization trap in disguise: nothing on disk references the shader or font those components need, so the Android build strips both and the Editor never shows it.

Case study (#291): the Settings panel (#219) — the game's first runtime-built UGUI (HUD/onboarding are IMGUI) — shipped as a magenta box with invisible text. Two independent causes:

  • The UI shader was stripped. A plain Image renders through the default UI material → the built-in UI/Default shader. It lives in unity_builtin_extra (GUID 0000000000000000f000000000000000) and must be listed in ProjectSettings/GraphicsSettings.asset → m_AlwaysIncludedShaders or it is dropped from the build → every Image renders Unity's missing-shader magenta. Verified built-in UGUI shader fileIDs (from real project files — do not guess, the YAML carries no name comment): 10770 = UI/Default, 10753 = Sprites/Default.
  • The font was Editor-only. Resources.GetBuiltinResource<Font>("LegacyRuntime.ttf") works in the Editor but is not build-reliable → labels draw nothing on device. Fix: bundle a real, license-clean .ttf under a Resources/ folder (with includeFontData: 1 in its committed .meta) and Resources.Load<Font> it. Watch glyph coverage — the bundled font must actually contain every glyph the UI uses (e.g. DejaVu Sans has ✕ U+2715 but not the fullwidth plus U+FF0B).

Guard both at the serialization level: assert the UI/Default entry is present in the GraphicsSettings.asset YAML text, and assert the font's .meta carries includeFontData: 1 at its pinned GUID. Assets/Tests/EditMode/UiBuildResourcesTests.cs is the reference implementation. This is build-only — EditMode/CI can't reproduce Android shader stripping, so an on-device playtest is the final confirmation.

docs.title: 6. Simulate the assertions before pushing
docs.text: The sandbox can't run Unity, but every serialization-level assertion is plain text matching — simulate the exact regexes/contains-checks against the final files with a quick Python script before committing. This proves red→green locally-in-spirit and catches regex/formatting mistakes without burning a ~5-minute CI round trip. (YAML formatting details matter: e.g. Unity writes a trailing space after empty scalar keys like m_SubKind: — copy formatting exactly.)

docs.title: Checklist for a new hand-authored block
docs.text:
• [ ] Found ≥1 real-world file containing the same block; copied key names, value shapes, sibling keys, ordering
  • [ ] Every enum value confirmed from a real file (not guessed, not from memory)
  • [ ] Any GUID-referenced asset has a committed .meta with pinned GUID (and pinned sprite internal ID if referenced as a Sprite)
  • [ ] Serialization-level EditMode guard test written first, asserting exact values
  • [ ] Assertions simulated against the final files before pushing
  • [ ] Report states plainly what only CI / a device can confirm

docs.title: Version source of truth
docs.text:
The app version lives in a plain VERSION file at the repo root, which release-please updates directly. The build script reads this file and injects the value into Unity's PlayerSettings (bundle version) at build time. (#73)

This was chosen over having release-please patch Unity's ProjectSettings/ProjectSettings.asset directly, since that file is large and riskier for automated text patching.

VERSION's content is the bare semver followed by a marker comment:

0.2.0 # x-release-please-version

The marker is required — release-please's generic extra-files updater (used for any file without a recognized JSON/YAML/TOML/XML extension) only rewrites a line that contains x-release-please-version; it does not blindly overwrite a file's entire contents. Without the marker, the updater has nothing to match and silently leaves the file untouched. This is exactly what happened in #114: VERSION stayed on 0.1.0 across a real 0.2.0 release because it was a bare version string with no marker, even though release-please's own manifest.json bookkeeping had correctly advanced. Anything that reads VERSION (build workflows, docs publishing) strips everything from # onward before parsing, so the trailing comment never leaks into a versionName/versionCode.

docs.title: Milestone versions vs. the shipped version
docs.text: GitHub milestones are version-named (v0.4, v1.0, …) as planning targets — see Conventions. Those labels are decoupled from the version release-please computes here: VERSION advances from Conventional-Commit history, so a milestone titled v0.4 describes a scope, and the version that actually ships when its work lands need not be exactly 0.4.0. Milestones plan; release-please versions. We deliberately don't add tooling to force the two to line up.

docs.title: release-please configuration
docs.text:
Config lives at non-default paths:

  • .github/release-please/config.json
  • .github/release-please/manifest.json

Settings:

  • release-type: simple, with an extra-files entry declaring VERSION explicitly as {"type": "generic", "path": "VERSION"} (release-please would infer the generic updater for an extensionless file either way, but spelling it out documents which updater applies and that VERSION therefore needs the x-release-please-version marker described above)
  • bump-minor-pre-major: false
  • bump-patch-for-minor-pre-major: false — standard semver: a feat: commit bumps minor even pre-1.0.0

Requires Conventional Commits (feat:, fix:, etc.) to be followed consistently, since release-please's version computation depends on them. A CI check lints PR titles against this (#82) so it doesn't rely on manual discipline alone.

A Core guard test (CoreTests/Doggiehood.Core.Tests/Versioning/VersionFileGuardTests.cs) asserts VERSION contains a valid bare semver and matches manifest.json's tracked version, so the two can't silently drift apart again the way they did in #114.

docs.title: One issue → one PR → one squash commit → one changelog entry
docs.text:
The issue pipeline's nightly dev run builds each selected issue on its own branch and opens one PR per issue — never a combined PR batching several issues together. This keeps release-please's changelog granular through the repository's squash-merge setting without any fragile PR-body trickery:

  • PR title = that issue's single Conventional-Commit line (e.g. feat: give approach-to-rest real walk-to-decoration movement). This is what pr-title-lint checks, and — because the PR resolves exactly one issue — it is also the natural subject of the squash commit that lands on main.
  • Squash commit = one Conventional Commit. release-please parses that single header and emits exactly one clean changelog entry for the issue. No extra Conventional lines are smuggled through the PR body, so nothing can be silently dropped by the squash the way a combined multi-issue PR did (#213).
  • PR body carries the required ## Deviations and Decisions section plus a Closes #N line so merging auto-closes the issue (see Development Agent & Workflow). The body is documentation for the reviewer, not a changelog-assembly mechanism.

Because each issue now lands as its own squash commit, main gains one commit per merged issue rather than one per multi-issue batch. Android's versionCode (derived below as git rev-list --count main) therefore rises one-per-issue — a smaller, steadier increment that is still strictly monotonic and deterministic.

docs.title: Android version code
docs.text: Android's versionCode (a plain incrementing integer, separate from the human-readable versionName) is derived at build time as git rev-list --count main — deterministic and always increasing, independent of CI run-number state. (#81)

docs.title: Docs versioning
docs.text: This documentation site is deployed with mike, tagged to the same version as the app (from the VERSION file / release tags) so historical doc versions stay browsable alongside the current one. See CI/CD for the publish workflow.

docs.title: GitHub is the source of truth for decisions; this site is the summary
docs.text: New ideas, open questions, and brainstorming happen as conversation and get captured as GitHub issues right away. This documentation site is the clean, current distillation of whatever's been decided — it's rewritten as decisions change, while the GitHub issues stay as the historical record of how each decision was reached.

docs.title: Labels
docs.text:
• area:* — what part of the game an issue touches: gameplay, art, audio, ui, story, build, ai.
  • type:* — epic (a tracking issue with sub-issues), task, question, bug.
  • No label for who owns a decision — Derek and Lucas both weigh in on everything; area: is enough to know what kind of decision it is.

docs.title: Pipeline labels
docs.text:
These labels are the state machine for the AI issue-management pipeline — a routine moves issues between them in response to Derek's issue-comment commands:

  • ai-triage — admitted for AI analysis.
  • pending-approval — analysis done; awaiting Derek's /approve.
  • needs-clarification — analysis posted a question; awaiting an answer.
  • ready-for-work — approved and milestoned; in the nightly dev queue. Invariant: ready-for-work ⇒ the issue has a milestone — the gatekeeper refuses an /approve that resolves no milestone (inline /milestone, the issue's current milestone, or the analysis-proposed one) and asks which milestone instead, so the focus-milestone-only nightly builder never silently skips an approved issue (#247).
  • in-progress — a nightly dev run has picked it up.
  • parked — hidden from every routine and the dashboard.
  • dashboard — marks the single live dashboard issue; excluded from every routine, except that /focus is honored on it so focus can be set from the dashboard itself (#204).

docs.title: Milestones are version-numbered scopes
docs.text:
Each milestone's title is a version (v0.4, v1.0, v1.1, v2.0, …) and its description carries the scope — what that version adds, expands, or polishes. Pick a milestone by matching an issue against the milestone's scope description, read live, rather than a memorized phase list.

These version numbers are planning labels, not release numbers. The shipped app version lives in /VERSION and is computed by release-please from Conventional Commits; a milestone titled v0.4 is a target scope, and the actual version that ships when its work lands may differ. The two are deliberately decoupled.

Milestones are forward-looking planning buckets. A version that has already shipped lives as a git tag / GitHub release, not a milestone — so there is no v0.3 milestone once v0.3 is out; any remaining open work simply moves to the next planning milestone.

Read the current milestones live — this page deliberately does not list them. The milestone set turns over constantly (versions ship and close, new ones spin up), so any table baked in here goes stale fast and mis-routes work — enumerate them and you will be matching against a snapshot months out of date. To see the live milestones and their scopes, use the milestone-ops skill:

python3 .claude/skills/milestone-ops/milestone_ops.py list

That lists every milestone with its state and open/closed counts; fetch the milestones REST endpoint (GET /repos/derekwinters/lucas-doggiehood/milestones?state=open) when you also need each one's scope description. Match an issue against the live scope description, never a memorized ladder.

New version milestones (v0.13, v0.14, …) are spun up as needed — each with its own focus (new functionality, playtest fixes, a larger map expansion) — rather than following a fixed pre-planned ladder.

Closing a milestone to new work. When a version is done taking new issues, freeze it: mark its GitHub milestone description as closed to new issues, and give the next milestone the active scope. Issue analysis proposes a milestone by matching an issue against these live scope descriptions (pipeline-analysis), so freezing one and activating the next is what reroutes new intake — existing approved issues in the frozen milestone stay put and finish, only new issues are redirected. /focus still controls which milestone the nightly builder works from; move it forward once the frozen milestone's ready-for-work queue drains. (This is a soft, description-driven convention, not a hard gate — an owner /approve or /milestone can still place an issue anywhere.)

Two non-version milestones sit alongside these:

  • Direct Involvement Needed — tasks no agent can complete (asset creation, on-device checks, unanswered questions). Not a version; excluded from version ordering.
  • The early setup and shipped phase milestones (00–08) remain closed as historical record; they are not renamed to versions.

Nightly development targets one focus milestone at a time (set with /focus <version>; see the issue pipeline).

docs.title: Every issue names the spec pages it touches
docs.text: An issue that changes player-facing behavior, layout, or a design decision should name — in its body or checklist — which docs/specs (or docs/engineering) page(s) it expects to update, or note that none apply. This makes the spec reconciliation a planned deliverable rather than an afterthought: the matching page is updated in the same PR as the code (a non-negotiable rule), and CI's always-on docs-test gate forces a conscious decision — a code-only PR fails unless it carries the skip-docs label.

docs.title: Epics and sub-issues
docs.text: A design area gets an epic issue (e.g. "Epic: Dog NPC Behavior") whose body is a short overview. Individual decisions are filed as sub-issues of that epic, one decision per issue, so the epic's checklist shows progress at a glance.

docs.title: When a question closes vs. stays open
docs.text:
• If the answer to an OPEN QUESTION issue is itself content that still needs to be built (a spec, a list, a roster, a number) — it gets updated with the decision and stays open until that content actually exists in the project.
  • It only closes when the real, ongoing tracking work has moved entirely into other already-open issues (for example, a resolved scope question that spawned a whole new epic).

docs.title: Docs versioning
docs.text: This site is built with MkDocs + Material for MkDocs, deployed with mike so multiple versions of the docs stay browsable side by side, tagged to match the game's own version (from the root VERSION file / release-please tags — see Versioning & Releases). See CI/CD for how the site builds and publishes.

docs.title: How to Play
docs.text: This describes the player-facing experience as currently designed. It's written from the player's point of view — for the underlying rules a developer implements against, see the linked spec pages.

docs.title: Exploring
docs.text: You view the neighborhood from an angled, isometric top-down camera — like looking down at a diorama. Drag to pan around, pinch to zoom in and out. There's no on-screen avatar; you interact directly with the world by tapping on it. The app runs in landscape. (Spec: Camera, Navigation & Controls)

docs.title: Meeting the dogs
docs.text:
Dogs live at houses around the neighborhood and wander the streets nearby. Some are inside, looking out a window. Each dog has a breed, a name, and a personality — a Brave dog acts differently than a Shy one, and (eventually) even walks differently. (Spec: Dog Behavior, Dog Roster & Names)

A dog with something to say shows a speech bubble above it. Tap the bubble to start a short conversation — the dog explains what it needs, you tap to help, done. No branching conversation trees, no quest log to check — the speech bubble is the only signal you need. (Spec: Conversation System)

docs.title: Helping out
docs.text:
A dog's request is one of a few kinds:

  • Lost something — a toy, or its own puppy — hidden somewhere in the visible neighborhood. Pan and zoom around until you spot it, then tap it.
  • Wants something bought — a toy, a pool, a comfort item for its yard. Accept, and a delivery truck drives up and drops the package at the dog's door. The dog itself heads home and sits waiting for it.
  • Has a bug problem — spray to clear it out.

Every completed request pays out a small amount of coin. (Spec: Quest & Economy, Quest Content)

docs.title: Spending coin
docs.text: Coin goes toward gifts for dogs and comfort decorations for their yards — a bed, a cushion, a blanket that the dog will wander over and use on its own from time to time. Decorations make a dog visibly happier, though happiness is flavor, not a mechanic you need to manage. Whatever you deliver stays in the world for good. (Spec: Decorations)

docs.title: Starting small
docs.text: The very first neighborhood is deliberately tiny: one intersection, two streets, four houses. Expanding to new streets and zones is real, planned, and fully designed — slated for v0.4. (Spec: Neighborhood Expansion — v0.4)

docs.title: The pitch
docs.text:
Doggiehood is a neighborhood of dogs, viewed from above. You don't control a character — you're an unseen presence panning and zooming around the streets, tapping on dogs who have something to say. Some dogs wander the sidewalks. Some watch from a window. Each one has a name, a breed, and a personality that colors how it talks and what it asks for.

Helping a dog — finding what it lost, buying what it wants, clearing out its bug problem — earns a little currency, which goes right back into the neighborhood: gifts for dogs, comfort decorations for their yards, and (in v0.4) whole new streets.

docs.title: Tone
docs.text:
• Cozy, not competitive. No fail states, no timers, no punishment for ignoring a quest. (#28)
  • All-ages. Built for a family to enjoy together, not designed around any one age bracket specifically. (#43)
  • A real place, not a store. Free, offline, no ads, no accounts. (#41, #42)
  • Bright and a little goofy. Bold saturated color, chunky sticker-book UI, a whimsical soundtrack — see Art & UI Style.

docs.title: Where the name comes from
docs.text: "Doggiehood" — a neighborhood of dogs. The starting cast (Zeus, Nala, Bailey, Sunny, Pepper, Duke, Scout, Waffles) and a set of easter-egg dogs named after real dogs Lucas knows are detailed in Dog Roster & Names.

docs.title: Who's building it, and how
docs.text: Derek handles structural/technical decisions; Lucas drives creative direction on the dogs, quests, and world. Design conversations happen live and get distilled into GitHub issues immediately, organized under epics and numbered milestones. See Project Conventions for how that organization works, and Engineering for how the actual Unity project gets built — by a dedicated development agent working test-first against those issues, not hand-written by either of them.

docs.title: Design & Architecture Specs
docs.text:
This section is the implementation contract. Each page is a settled design area; every rule on it has already been decided (traceable to a GitHub issue) and is either fully specified or explicitly flagged as a placeholder pending real content.

A development agent implementing a feature should treat these pages as authoritative. If something needed to implement a feature isn't covered here, that's a gap — stop and flag it rather than inventing a rule, and it should get resolved back in GitHub first.

docs.title: v1.0 scope
docs.text: v1.0 — the first complete release — integrates all mainline functionality into one playable build across the 4 starting houses, with real art, polish, and onboarding. The bulk of that functionality lands first in graybox under v0.4, which now also includes neighborhood expansion (#88) — the Neighborhood Expansion page is fully designed and no longer deferred. See Conventions for the version-milestone model.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text:
World

  • World & Neighborhood — the physical setting
  • Camera, Navigation & Controls — how the player sees and moves
  • Art & UI Style — palette, architecture, and interface chrome
  • Sidewalks & Walk Network — sidewalk placement, crosswalks, and how dogs pathfind

Dogs

  • Dog Behavior — how dogs move, live, and act
  • Dog Roster & Names — the starting cast and the naming system

Conversation & Quests

  • Conversation System — talking to a dog
  • Quest & Economy — the core play loop and currency
  • Quest Content — the actual quest types

UI Wireframes

  • UI Wireframes Overview — the layout contract for every screen, panel, and overlay (see the UI Design Process)
  • Shared UI Components — reusable atomic pieces referenced by every screen

Other systems

  • Decorations
  • Neighborhood Expansion (v0.4)
  • Audio
  • Onboarding
  • Product Scope & Constraints
  • Future Ideas (explicitly out of scope, kept for later)

docs.title: Audio
docs.text:
Epic: #16

An upbeat, cozy/whimsical soundtrack matching the low-poly cheerful art style, plus playful sound effects for barks, the delivery truck, item pickups, and other interactions. (#40)

No specific tracks or SFX assets exist yet — this is a direction, not a delivered asset list.

docs.title: Build checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Background music track(s) in a cozy/whimsical style, looping cleanly
  • [ ] SFX: dog bark, delivery truck arrival, item pickup/delivery, UI tap/confirm
  • [ ] Audio can be muted independently of the rest of the app (standard mobile expectation, not separately tracked as an issue but assumed)

docs.title: Decorations
docs.text: Epic: #45

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: Decorations apply to a specific dog's own yard/house only. No decorating shared public spaces (streets, the intersection) for v1.0. (#46)

docs.title: Effect
docs.text: Decorations are cosmetic but also raise a dog's happiness. Happiness affects animations (more wagging), idle behavior, and dialogue tone/mood only — it never gates or unlocks quests, dialogue, or rewards. This keeps the no-fail, low-pressure design intact. (#47)

docs.title: Placement
docs.text: Decorations are placed automatically in a sensible spot in the yard — no drag-and-drop or arranging UI for v1.0. (#48)

docs.title: Capacity (= house level)
docs.text:
A yard holds at most as many decorations as its house level — 1 at level 1, up to 4 at level 4 (#59). A placement past the current capacity is rejected. Upgrading the house raises the cap.

Grandfathering (Derek, 2026-07-14): the MVP decoration flow auto-placed with no cap, so a yard can already hold more decorations than its level allows when the cap ships. Nothing already placed is ever removed — the cap blocks new placements only. In Core this is GameState.TryAddDecoration (the capacity-respecting path); the raw AddDecoration used by save-load stays uncapped, which is what preserves the grandfathered items.

docs.title: Acquisition
docs.text:
There is no standalone decoration shop. Decorations are requested by dogs the same way other gifts are, as part of the normal quest rotation, fulfilled via the delivery truck (see Quest Content). (#49)

A decoration request is generic (e.g. "my yard could use something comfy") rather than naming one specific item — the player picks which item to send from a small set of options. This differs from the toy/pool quest, which asks for one specific named thing. (#50)

docs.title: v1.0 category: comfort items
docs.text:
Starting scope is comfort items — dog beds, cushions, blankets. (#51) Other categories considered for later: play items (pool, sprinkler), yard dressing (flowers, fence), food/bowls.

Once delivered, the dog periodically decides — on its own, no player tap/trigger, consistent with dogs already behaving autonomously — to walk over to the comfort item and settle onto it. The dog actually paths there over the walk network (sidewalks, crosswalks, its house's front walkway) from wherever it is, then enters the "Rest" pose on arrival — it never teleports into the pose. (#52, #112) See the "Rest" pose in Dog Behavior.

docs.title: Build checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Decoration requests are scoped to a single dog's own yard; no shared-space decorating exists
  • [ ] Delivering a decoration raises the dog's happiness value; happiness only affects animation/dialogue tone, never gameplay gating
  • [ ] Decorations auto-place in the yard on delivery — no placement UI
  • [ ] Decoration requests come from the same quest rotation as other requests, not a separate shop screen
  • [ ] A decoration request presents a small set of item choices (not one named item) for the player to pick from
  • [ ] At least the 3 comfort items (bed, cushion, blanket) exist as deliverable decorations
  • [ ] A dog with a comfort decoration periodically and automatically walks over to it via the walk network and uses the "Rest" pose on it on arrival (no teleport into the pose)

docs.title: Neighborhood Expansion
docs.text:
Epic: #55

v0.4

This entire system is fully designed and is now slated for v0.4 (#88) — no longer deferred. The neighborhood still starts with just the 4 houses (see World & Neighborhood); nothing on this page gets built before v0.4 starts.

docs.title: The loop
docs.text:
1. Unlock a zone: the player pays a currency cost to unlock a new zone/area of the map. Newly unlocked zones start with no houses at all — just empty land. (#56)
  2. Build houses: the player spends currency to construct individual houses within an unlocked zone. Houses don't appear automatically — building each one is its own purchase. (#57)
  3. Vacancy: a freshly built house is empty and renders greyscaled until a dog eventually moves in. (#58)
  4. Occupancy over time: new dogs arrive and move into empty houses gradually over time, rather than all at once. (#54) See Move-in system below for the full mechanism, and Dog Roster & Names for how names and breeds are drawn.
  5. House leveling: every house starts at level 1 and can be upgraded up to level 4. Upgrading makes the house visually bigger/nicer and increases how many decorations its yard can hold. (#59)

docs.title: Map shape
docs.text:
Decision (2026-07-31, Derek, on #295) — player-choice single-tile frontier, superseding the sequential-zone model below. The unlock unit is a single tile, not a hand-grouped zone, and the order is the player's choice. Any placed tile's open road edge that borders a tile defined in the full authored target map (docs/tools/map-data.json, #383) and not yet placed is an unlockable frontier coordinate — shown with a lock icon the player can tap to unlock if they can afford it. The frontier is derived algorithmically from (placed map) vs (target map) using #109 edge-adjacency — a candidate must both place validly (TileMap.CanPlace) and carry a real road connection into the network (TileMap.HasRoadConnectionAt — at least one shared edge with a road on both sides, added #507), so no manual grouping/carving is authored and no lock icon appears on a tile with no road leading into it. Onboarding gate: before the onboarding reward-chain's step-3 "expand the map" completes, only that one scripted tile is unlockable; after it completes, every current frontier tile is simultaneously unlockable, in any order. This supersedes the "unlock authored zones in sequence" model described in the 2026-07-14 decision immediately below and its ZoneCatalog-list implementation. The multi-lock indicator rework (one lock per open connection point) shipped in #453, which also RETIRED the legacy sequential path outright — ZoneCatalog, Zone/ZoneTilePlacement, TryUnlockNextZone, ZoneUnlock/ZoneUnlockNumbers/ZoneUnlockOffer, RestoreUnlockedZoneCount, and the single-marker indicator (ExpansionIndicator.Resolve(state), ExpansionIndicatorPlacement.Resolve(map, zone)) are all deleted. Frontier tiles now cover the same ground: the Unity layer supplies the authored target map at runtime (MapDataLoader loads Assets/Resources/Data/map-data.json and calls SetTargetMap at bootstrap), each frontier tile's lots get stable house ids from a pure FrontierHouseId.For(coordinate, quadrant) function, and ExpansionUnlockDirector maintains one lock indicator per unlockable frontier coordinate. Old saves are not carried across this change (a legacy zones=N line is simply no longer understood); the onboarding single-tile gate (only (0,1) unlockable until the "expand the map" step completes) is unchanged.

Decision (2026-07-14, Derek, on #86) — superseded for unlock unit/order by the 2026-07-31 decision above; still current that expansion is authored, not procedural. the map is hand-picked expansion with no fixed end — tiles are authored and added over time, and procedural generation stays out of scope (#109). The authored tiles come from the tile catalog (60m grid), pre-authored by Derek and Lucas; the player never freely places arbitrary tiles — they only unlock tiles the authored target map already defines. Early tiles use only cul-de-sac, straight, tee, and turn tiles — more variety comes later. (That variety was originally to include the OpposingTurns/park-island tiles; those types were removed from the catalog outright by #583 — see Tile Catalog.) (Original wording: a zone was a hand-authored group of tiles unlocked in sequence; the 2026-07-31 decision replaced the group with a single tile and the sequence with player choice.)

First zone: a single cul-de-sac directly north of the starting intersection. The confirmed layout (2026-07-29, Derek, on #360): from the starting FourWay at grid (0,0), a single CulDeSacSouth tile at (0,1) — its road enters from the south edge (meeting the origin FourWay's north road) and ends in a bulb pointing north, so the whole zone sits due north with no dangling roads. This supersedes the earlier two-tile northwest layout (2026-07-14, Derek, on #56: TurnSW at (0,1) + CulDeSacEast at (−1,1), which ran north then turned west into the bulb) — the single north tile also lines up straight under the expansion lock indicator, which already hovers due north of the origin.

The tile-grid placement/adjacency system this all sits on is #109, the milestone's geometric prerequisite.

Implementation note (#383) — the authored target map is loadable in Core. The full neighborhood Derek & Lucas authored in the Map Builder (84 tiles, committed as design data at docs/tools/map-data.json, shaped {name, tiles:[{x,y,type}]} with x→Col, y→Row and origin FourWay at (0,0)) parses into a validated Core TileMap via Doggiehood.Core.World.MapDefinition.Parse + MapLoader.Load, exposed as the neighborhood's target/full layout. Placement is self-ordered — the file lists tiles in authoring order, not adjacency order, so the loader seeds the origin then repeatedly places any pending tile that already has a placed neighbour (through #109's TileMap.CanPlace/Place) until nothing more can be placed; a tile that fails adjacency is reported in MapLoadResult.RejectedCoordinates, never thrown. MapLoadResult.CurvedCorners gives, per bend (Turn*) tile, the Quadrant corner that renders curved (data only — no rendering yet). This is Option A of #383: the loader produces the target map as Core data; the live playable world stays incremental (seeded FourWay, grown one tile at a time). The target map is now the reference the player-choice frontier unlock (#295) reads: GameState.SetTargetMap supplies it, and Doggiehood.Core.Expansion.TileFrontier.Compute(placed, target) derives the unlockable coordinates from it — see the #295 note under Pricing.

docs.title: Green-space tiles (auto-activated)
docs.text:
Decision (2026-08-05, Derek, /approved on #539) — green spaces are free auto-activations, not paid frontier unlocks. A "green-space tile" is the new 18th TileType.GreenSpace: a full grid tile authored into the target map (docs/tools/map-data.json) like any other type, but carrying no road and no lots. It is not part of the paid, road-connected frontier above — instead it auto-activates for free (no coin cost, no lock icon) the instant 2 or more of its 4 edges border an already-activated tile, where "activated" means any tile currently on the live Map — a placed road tile or an already-activated green space. Activation cascades unbounded to a fixpoint: one freshly activated green space can give an adjacent green space its second bordering edge, and the whole connected blob turns on in a single pass (Derek's "if that cascades into a bunch of green space that's okay, as long as it's always the 2-tile touching rule").

Implementation note (#539). Built as pure Core logic, deliberately separate from TileFrontier/TryUnlockTile:

  • Eligibility — Doggiehood.Core.Expansion.GreenSpaceActivation.Compute(placed, target) returns every target GreenSpace coordinate not yet placed whose count of edges bordering a placed.HasTileAt neighbour is ≥ 2 (same shape as TileFrontier.Compute, but keyed on the 2-edge rule instead of a road connection).
  • Activation pass — GameState runs a pass that loops GreenSpaceActivation.Compute + TileMap.Place to a fixpoint (not a single hop), invoked after a successful TryUnlockTile (a road placement can newly qualify green neighbours) and once inside SetTargetMap (the single "after target-map/save restore" hook). Green spaces are placed straight onto Map without being recorded in UnlockedTiles: they are not player unlocks, carry no lots, and — see persistence — are re-derived rather than persisted.
  • Free / no cost curve inflation — no Wallet interaction at all. The road-unlock cost curve scales on RoadTileCount (non-GreenSpace tiles on Map) rather than raw Map.Tiles.Count, so the free green spaces that also grow Map.Tiles never inflate the price of the next road unlock. With no green space placed this equals Map.Tiles.Count, so pre-#539 pricing is unchanged.
  • Frontier exclusion (no lock icon) — a GreenSpace tile carries zero road edges, so it can never satisfy TileMap.HasRoadConnectionAt and is structurally excluded from TileFrontier/UnlockableFrontier(); a regression test pins that it never appears there even when bordering 2+ placed tiles.
  • Persistence — pure replay, no new save format. Activation is a pure function of the already-persisted placed road tiles, so nothing green is written to the save (no green= line; green coordinates are absent from the tile= set). On load the existing tile= road lines replay onto Map, then the SetTargetMap activation pass re-derives exactly the same green-space membership.
  • Unity — a placed GreenSpace tile needs no new rendering: WorldBuilder's road-art/lot/tree passes iterate UnlockedTiles (which never includes a green space), so they no-op for it, while ResizeGroundToMap grows the grass ground plane to cover it because it sizes from the whole Map.

docs.title: Pricing
docs.text:
Decisions 2026-07-14 (Derek, in conversation). All values are named, tunable constants in Core — expect adjustment during playtesting; see also Quest & Economy.

Purchase Cost Tile unlock (frontier) 50-coin base + 10 per already-unlocked tile (#295, rebalanced #540): TileUnlockNumbers.BaseCost (50) + PerExistingTileStep (10) × player-unlocked tiles, no cap — the first unlock matches a house build, then each rises by 10 (Derek's "+10 per existing tile"). The origin FourWay is excluded, so the first unlock is at the base. A single swappable balance function (TileUnlock.Cost(placedTileCount)). Supersedes and (as of #453) fully replaces the earlier escalating zone-unlock formula (100, 200, 300, …); the ZoneUnlock path is deleted. Build a house 50-coin base + 5 per 4 houses built (#57, rebalanced #540): HouseBuildNumbers.BaseCost (50) + PerBatchStep (5) × floor(playerBuiltHouses / HousesPerStep) (4), no cap — builds 1-4 at 50, 5-8 at 55, and so on. The 4 starting houses are excluded, so the first build is at the base. HouseBuildNumbers.Cost(housesBuilt). House upgrade to L2 / L3 / L4 100 / 200 / 400 coins (doubles per level)

Rebalance (2026-08-03, Derek, on #540) — cheaper starting expansion + gentle cost-scaling. Plain English: the first tile unlock now costs the same as a house (50, down from a flat 100), so the early game opens up a bit faster; after that, both sinks scale so growth still can't run away. Tile unlocks climb +10 per tile already unlocked and house builds climb +5 for every 4 houses built. Counts are player actions only — the origin FourWay and the 4 starting houses don't count, so the first unlock and first build are both at the 50 base. Neither curve is capped (flat-then-linear). Both live as named, tunable balance functions in Core (TileUnlock.Cost / HouseBuildNumbers.Cost) for one-place future tuning.

Implementation note (#56) — HISTORICAL; the Zone/ZoneCatalog sequential-unlock machinery below was RETIRED by #453. It is superseded end-to-end by the player-choice frontier (TryUnlockTile, FrontierHouseId, UnlockedTiles) described in the #295 and #453 notes above; the classes named here (Zone, ZoneCatalog, ZoneUnlock, TryUnlockNextZone, RestoreUnlockedZoneCount) no longer exist. Kept for provenance: built as pure Core logic on top of #109's tile grid — Doggiehood.Core.World.Zone (authored tile placements + the quadrant lots each tile carries, via TileLotCatalog/TileGeometry), Doggiehood.Core.World.ZoneCatalog (the authored zone list — only the first zone exists yet), and Doggiehood.Core.Expansion.ZoneUnlock/ZoneUnlockNumbers for the cost formula. GameState now owns a TileMap (Map, seeded with just the starting FourWay intersection) and UnlockedZones; GameState.TryUnlockNextZone() is the one entry point — it charges Wallet for the next zone in sequence, adds that zone's tiles to Map through #109's placement/adjacency validation, and returns false with no state change (no deduction, no tiles placed) if the balance can't cover it or every authored zone is already unlocked. Unlocking never creates House objects — GameState.IsLotBuildable(houseId) reports a zone's lots as buildable exactly because no House exists for that id yet, which is what house building (#57) checks. Persistence (#343): Map/UnlockedZones now round-trip through SaveCodec so an unlocked zone survives an app relaunch. Because zones are authored and deterministic (ZoneCatalog), the save stores only the unlocked count (zones=N); on load GameState.RestoreUnlockedZoneCount replays the first N authored zones onto Map/UnlockedZones without re-charging the wallet or re-advancing the reward chain (the parallel of RestoreRewardChainStep). A legacy save with no zones line loads as nothing unlocked.

Implementation note (#295) — the player-choice frontier unlock (supersedes the sequential zone unlock above). Built as pure Core logic: Doggiehood.Core.Expansion.TileFrontier.Compute(placed, target) returns every coordinate that (a) borders an already-placed tile, (b) exists in the authored target map, (c) isn't already placed, (d) would place validly (TileMap.CanPlace — its road/no-road edges agree with every placed neighbour), and (e) forms a real road connection into the network (TileMap.HasRoadConnectionAt — at least one shared edge carries a road on both sides). Requirement (e) is what makes the frontier precisely Derek's "a road with a connection point that has another tile defined": CanPlace alone (corrected #507) is satisfied just as well by a no-road/no-road boundary, so keying the lock indicator to edge-agreement without (e) surfaced lock icons on tiles with no road leading into them. CanPlace's broader edge-agreement semantics stay unchanged everywhere else (e.g. MapLoader's authored-map placement replay), which legitimately relies on no-road/no-road edges agreeing. GameState gains the authored TargetMap (supplied by the Unity layer via SetTargetMap; not itself persisted — fixed design data re-supplied each launch), UnlockedTiles (the coordinates unlocked one-at-a-time), and UnlockableFrontier() (the frontier gated by onboarding: only the single scripted OnboardingExpansionTile — the authored first tile at (0,1) — until the reward-chain "expand the map" step completes, then the whole frontier at once). GameState.TryUnlockTile(coordinate) is the one entry point — it charges Doggiehood.Core.Expansion.TileUnlock.Cost(placedTileCount) (a single, named, swappable balance function — since #540 TileUnlockNumbers.BaseCost = 50 plus PerExistingTileStep = 10 per player-unlocked tile, the origin FourWay excluded so the first unlock is at the base; callers thread the live Map.Tiles.Count), places the chosen frontier tile through #109's validated TileMap.Place, and advances the onboarding "expand the map" step; it returns false with no state change (no deduction, no tile placed) when the coordinate isn't a currently-unlockable frontier tile or the balance can't cover the cost. Persistence: unlocked tiles round-trip through SaveCodec as the actual set of unlocked coordinates (tile=col|row|type, emitted in unlock order), superseding the sequential zones=N count for the frontier path; on load GameState.RestoreUnlockedTile replaces each onto Map without re-charging the wallet. #453 wired the Unity layer to this frontier model (multiple simultaneous locks, one per open connection point) and deleted the legacy zones=N/TryUnlockNextZone/ZoneCatalog path — see the #453 note under Frontier-tile lots and the map-shape decision above.

docs.title: Frontier-tile lots and house ids
docs.text:
Implementation note (#453) — frontier tiles grow buildable lots. A player-unlocked frontier tile carries the quadrant lots its type defines (TileLotCatalog.LotsFor, generic across every lotted type — the 16 road tiles and, since #607, the full-intersection FourWay, which contributes its four quadrant lots like any other tile so an unlocked interior 4-way junction is buildable; only the origin FourWay is exempt, its four houses seeded from NeighborhoodLayout and guarded in GameState.LotsForUnlockedTile), positioned from the tile centre and given a stable, collision-free house id derived purely from (coordinate, quadrant) via Doggiehood.Core.World.FrontierHouseId.For (zig-zag-encode col/row, Cantor-pair them, * 4 + quadrantIndex, plus a fixed base offset clear of the 4 starting ids). Because the id is a pure function of position — not a replayable counter — the mapping needs no extra persistence and survives player-chosen unlock order. GameState.IsLotBuildable/GetHouseLot/TryBuildHouse resolve a frontier tile's lots (via GameState.LotsForUnlockedTile) exactly as they already do for a starting lot, and TryUnlockTile rolls + persists each new lot's HouseVariant at unlock (the frontier equivalent of the retired AssignZoneLotVariants), so an empty frontier lot renders its predetermined ladder/tint and pre-baked yard trees immediately. Every frontier id is ≥ HouseVariantAssignment.FirstZoneHouseId, so it rolls a variant like any zone house did.

Implementation note (#57, rebalanced #540): GameState.TryBuildHouse(houseId) is the one entry point — it charges Doggiehood.Core.Expansion.HouseBuildNumbers.Cost(GameState.PlayerBuiltHouseCount) (50-coin base + 5 per 4 player-built houses; the 4 starting houses excluded, so the first build is at the base) from Wallet and adds a new House at House.InitialLevel (1) and vacant, returning false with no state change when the lot already has a house (IsLotBuildable false), the lot's zone hasn't been unlocked yet, or the balance can't cover the cost. GameState.GetHouseLot(houseId) resolves a house's lot across both the starting layout and any unlocked zone, for the Unity layer. On the Unity side, WorldBuilder.BuildEmptyLots renders one graybox marker (EmptyLotView) per buildable lot in every unlocked zone; ExpansionDirector wires each marker's tap to the reusable confirmation dialog (Building a house first asks, #406): a tap resolves Doggiehood.Core.Expansion.HouseBuildOffer.Resolve(state, houseId) (null when the lot isn't buildable — a no-op that never opens the dialog) and raises the dialog with "Build a house here?" + the current scaled build cost (HouseBuildOffer.Resolve reads HouseBuildNumbers.Cost(PlayerBuiltHouseCount), #540) on Yes; only Yes calls TryBuildHouse, and on success replaces the marker with the real house visual (WorldBuilder.BuildHouse) and saves — No/scrim cancels with no spend. A mid-game build now also renders the lot's yard and fence (#405): after BuildHouse, ExpansionDirector calls the single-lot render helpers WorldBuilder.BuildYardLandscaping(lot) / BuildFence(lot) / BuildWalkway(lot) (extracted from the world-build loops), so a zone house gets its yard trees — and its fence when fences are visible — the same treatments a starting house gets at world-build time, instead of only its bare mesh. The full world-build and debug-toggle fence loops cover zone houses too (#424): WorldBuilder.BuildFences/RebuildFences iterate every built house via GameState.GetHouseLot rather than the starting-only NeighborhoodLayout.HouseLots, so a zone house is fenced on a fresh world build and when the #219 debug toggle rebuilds fences — not only at the moment it is built. The fence still stays hidden by default (HouseLot.HasFence off); #424 only makes the geometry exist and build for every house. A zone house now also faces the street with a real front walkway (#430) — the front-walkway/street-facing piece is no longer deferred. GameState.WalkNetwork admits a built zone house's lot (its filter widened to accept a house with an authored style or a rolled HouseVariant), so the lot grows a real front-walkway edge; the render path builds against that live network (ExpansionDirector and WorldBuilder.Build pass state.WalkNetwork into BuildHouse/BuildWalkway, calling the network-aware HousePlacement.FrontFacing(lot, network) overload) instead of the starting-tile-only NeighborhoodLayout.WalkNetwork, so the zone house renders facing its street with a tiled walkway to the door — a starting-house treatment — rather than the old Z-sign facing fallback / BuildWalkway no-op. A zone house's fence and yard trees now rotate with it too (#461): #430 threaded the live-network facing into the house mesh and its walkway only, so the fence (via the debug toggle) and the pre-baked trees still used the pre-rotation Z-sign fallback and sat at the old orientation. LotFence.GeometryFor(lot, state) now reads state.WalkNetwork for the fence's facing/position, and the yard-tree pre-bake (WorldBuilder.BuildEmptyLots/RenderUnlockedTile → the BuildYardLandscaping(lot, tileType, network) overload) threads that same live network so a zone lot's trees orient to the house's real street-ward facing. Because trees are baked at unlock before any walkway edge exists (below), the tree/fence path resolves the predetermined facing by projecting the lot centre onto its nearest sidewalk (HousePlacement.PredeterminedFrontFacing/PredeterminedPosition), which on this axis-aligned map equals the walkway-derived facing the build later resolves — so the pre-placed trees stay correct and are never regenerated (a Core test locks predetermined == actual, protecting #434's no-regenerate assumption). Letting the lot into WalkNetwork also puts its walkway on the graph dogs path over; a resident-only wander gate keeps every other dog off it (see the walk network and Dog Behavior pages). Dogs entering the house / passing through to the backyard stays out of scope (a possible later follow-up). A stray tap no longer spends coins, so building now mirrors the zone-unlock spend (both go through the same "are you sure?" dialog); the currency HUD reflects a confirmed build automatically since it reads Wallet.Coins live every frame. (House upgrade stays deliberately confirmation-free — Derek's Option A, #294 — so building is confirmed while upgrading is a direct spend.) Empty-lot marker look (settled, #300 (B), Derek; revised by #434): the marker is a low raised graybox "foundation" slab that reads as "a house goes here" — a single primitive box (WorldBuilder.EmptyLotFoundationSlabHeight tall, base flush on the ground plane, painted Palette.EmptyLotMarkerHex), no new kit asset. Its X/Z footprint is now sized to the predetermined house's level-1 mesh footprint and centred on it (#434), reversing the earlier #300 option-3 fixed-marker size (WorldBuilder.EmptyLotMarkerFootprint, now removed). The slab is oriented to the lot's real, network-resolved street-ward facing — not a fixed/default rotation (#569). #434 sized the marker from the single-arg HousePlacement.HouseFootprint(lot), which resolves facing via the starting-tile NeighborhoodLayout.WalkNetwork singleton and, for a zone lot with no walkway edge there, falls back to a Z-only guess — so whenever a lot's real facing is along X the slab's width/depth swapped onto the wrong axis (right size, transposed) relative to the house that gets built there (the same #461 bug class the yard trees already had). The empty-lot render sites (WorldBuilder.BuildEmptyLots on the initial build, RenderUnlockedTile on a mid-game unlock) now build the marker through the network-aware WorldBuilder.BuildEmptyLot(parent, lot, state.WalkNetwork) overload — resolving the footprint via HousePlacement.HouseFootprint(lot, network) (predetermined facing/position, the same live map-spanning network they already thread into BuildYardLandscaping) — so the foundation previews the house's actual facing. (A kept 2-arg BuildEmptyLot(parent, lot) overload retains the starting-network path for isolated call sites.) #300's reasoning — "an empty lot has no built house (no rolled model) to size a footprint from" — no longer holds: since #414 HouseModelCatalog.ForHouse is zone-aware (it resolves the rolled ladder's level-1 mesh instead of throwing for a zone lot id ≥ 5), and since #434 the variant is rolled and persisted at unlock (below), so an empty lot does know its future house. The lot also pre-places its yard trees at unlock (#434): the empty-lot render sites (WorldBuilder.BuildEmptyLots on the initial build, RenderUnlockedTile on a mid-game unlock) call the deterministic WorldBuilder.BuildYardLandscaping(lot) too, so an empty lot shows trees + a house-sized foundation, not a bare box. Building the lot then swaps only the foundation slab for the house mesh — the already-rendered trees are left in place (ExpansionDirector.ConfirmBuild deliberately does not re-render them), so there are no duplicates. Houses built this way have no authored HouseStyleTable entry (that table only covers the starting 4). Their look is designed and implemented (#299, Derek 2026-07-28; timing moved earlier by #434): each zone house rolls its own model ladder (one of five) and tint (one of a generated 20-color palette) via a deterministic seed on its house id (Doggiehood.Core.Art.HouseVariantAssignment), assigned when its tile unlocks (GameState.TryUnlockTile, stored in GameState.AssignedLotVariants) rather than lazily at build (#434), and persisted (ladder id + tint index) through SaveCodec (a lotvariant= line for an assigned-but-unbuilt lot; a built lot's variant rides its house= line) so it survives relaunch and L1→L4 upgrades. TryBuildHouse reads that pre-assignment; a legacy save whose zone predates #434 has no persisted entry and falls back to the same deterministic HouseVariantAssignment.ForHouse roll — bit-identical, since the roll is a pure function of the house id. WorldBuilder.BuildHouse renders the rolled ladder's current-level mesh and multiplies the palette tint over it (ApplyPaletteTint); the graybox fallback is now reached only when the kit model can't load or a house carries no rolled variant. See Art Style → House architecture for the full rule. The player-facing zone-unlock trigger ships in #343 — see Expansion indicator below.

docs.title: Move-in system
docs.text:
Decision 2026-07-14 (Derek, in conversation), detailed on #54. All values named, tunable constants; RNG injectable for deterministic tests.

  • Trigger — quest-completion pity counter, shared: every completed quest rolls a single shared move-in chance: a base chance plus a per-quest increment for every completed quest without a move-in, reset to base on success. One counter for the whole neighborhood; on success one vacant house is chosen at random (uniform). The counter only advances while at least one vacant house exists. Population-scaled rate (#625): the base and increment scale with the live dog count so move-ins are faster while the neighborhood is small and settle lower as it fills (population is the flywheel — it both is the "more dogs" goal and multiplies quest availability). Early (≤ 6 dogs): base 15%, +15%/quest. Late (≥ 20 dogs): base 5%, +5%/quest (the original values). Between the two the rate interpolates linearly, clamped outside the span. The rate is derived from the live dog count each roll — no new persisted state — and the mechanics are otherwise unchanged (still only on quest completion, only with a vacant house, still reset to the scaled base on success). All four curve endpoints plus the two population bounds are tunable TuningConfig fields, slider-exposed via the debug tuning menu.
  • Households: roster-style mix from day one — 70% single / 25% parent+puppy / 5% three-dog. Parent+puppy pairs share a breed; every dog gets its own personality, randomly drawn from the behavior set.
  • Breeds: the reserved French Bulldog and Puggle are the first two move-ins; afterwards breeds are chosen by count-weighted randomness — each breed weighted inversely by how many currently live in the neighborhood, so variety self-adapts to the existing distribution.
  • Easter eggs: each move-in has a 5% chance the household head is an easter-egg dog (fixed breed/coat, breed roll skipped); once used, an easter-egg name is permanently removed from the reserve — each appears exactly once.
  • Names come from the general name pool, no duplicates among active dogs.
  • New dogs join the daily quest rotation immediately.
  • Announcement: a move-in raises a "Welcome to the neighborhood!" celebration pop-up (one per household) — see the welcome pop-up wireframe for the layout, its per-dog member-chip row, timing, and the "Say hi!" camera pan.

Implementation note (#54/#58): the mechanism above is built as pure Core logic — Doggiehood.Core.Expansion.MoveInSystem, VacantHouses, and BreedWeighting — operating on an abstract set of vacant house ids plus the current dog roster, with no dependency on the #109/#56 tile-grid/zone geometry. Doggiehood.Core.World.House carries the vacancy flag itself (IsVacant, flipped by MarkOccupied); Doggiehood.Core.Expansion.HouseOccupancy bridges the two, deriving the current vacant set from live houses, running one MoveInSystem roll, and — only on success — occupying the filled house. GameState.HandleQuestCompleted calls this on every completed quest (QuestManager.Complete), so the trigger is fully wired. Since zone unlock (#56) and house building (#57) don't exist yet, every house in a real game is one of the 4 starting houses (already occupied at GameState.CreateNew()) — so this wiring has no vacant house to actually fill until #56/#57 land, but is exercised directly in the Core test suite. Persistence (#437): MoveInSystem's pity counter (quests-since-last-move-in, i.e. the accumulated move-in chance) and its consumed easter-egg / reserved-breed reserve now round-trip through SaveCodec — a single moveIn=<questsSinceLastMoveIn>|<remaining easter-egg names>|<remaining reserved breeds> line (breeds stored by name; a reserve segment is empty once exhausted). On load GameState.RestoreMoveInState rebuilds the system from those saved values without rolling any dice or firing a move-in (the parallel of RestoreRewardChainStep); a legacy save with no moveIn= line keeps CreateNew's default fresh system (the population-scaled base chance, 0 quests, full reserves). So move-in odds no longer reset to the base and a used easter-egg name never reappears across an app relaunch.

Implementation note (#625) — population-scaled rate. The pity counter's base and per-quest increment are no longer flat: MoveInNumbers.ScaledBaseMoveInChance(dogCount) / ScaledMoveInIncrementPerQuest(dogCount) interpolate linearly from the early (small-neighborhood) rate down to the late (settled) rate over the [MoveInEarlyPopulation, MoveInLatePopulation] span, clamped outside it. MoveInSystem.CurrentMoveInChance(dogCount) composes scaledBase + questsSinceLastMoveIn × scaledIncrement, and OnQuestCompleted threads the live roster size (activeDogs.Count, i.e. GameState.Dogs) into the roll — so the scaling is purely a function of the live dog count with no new persisted state (the moveIn= line is unchanged). The six curve parameters — EarlyMoveInChance/EarlyMoveInChanceIncrementPerQuest (early 15%/15%), BaseMoveInChance/MoveInChanceIncrementPerQuest (late 5%/5%, the original values), and MoveInEarlyPopulation/MoveInLatePopulation (6 / 20) — are TuningConfig fields surfaced through MoveInNumbers, so the debug tuning menu (#622) can retune the curve live. These are first-pass balance defaults, expected to be tuned on-device.

Implementation note (#436) — a move-in is reflected in-game the instant it happens. The Core mechanism above filled a vacant house but was invisible during play: QuestManager.Complete discarded HandleQuestCompleted's returned household, so the Unity layer never learned a dog had moved in — no DogView appeared and the filled house stayed greyscaled until a full world rebuild. Core now surfaces the event: QuestManager raises public event Action<IReadOnlyList<Dog>> MoveInOccurred from the single Complete funnel, right after HandleQuestCompleted, only when the returned household is non-empty — so all three completion paths (delivery, lost-item find, spray) are covered for free. On the Unity side QuestDirector subscribes in Init and, on each move-in, (a) spawns a DogView for every new resident — bound to the filled houseId, tappable and wandering — through the extracted DogSpawner.SpawnDog(state, parent, dog, indexAtHouse) (the per-dog body of the build-time SpawnDogs loop, so the live and build paths share identical house-lookup/stagger/DogView.Init wiring) without touching or duplicating any existing DogView, and (b) drops the filled house's vacancy greyscale (#58) by calling HouseUpgradeDirector.RefreshHouse(houseId) — the same destroy-and-rebuild the #407 upgrade path uses, which re-derives the mesh from the same Core House/HouseLot and so preserves the house's rolled variant/tint while the now-occupied flag makes the rebuild pick the normal tint instead of the grey. WorldBootstrap builds the HouseUpgradeDirector up front (moved earlier than #407's original profile-overlay closure) so QuestDirector.Init can hold a reference to it; its rebuild-callback (tap re-wiring) is still configured in BuildHouseProfileOverlay, which runs before any quest can complete. No save-format change — SaveStore/SaveCodec already persist Houses/Dogs, so a live move-in already round-trips; this issue is purely the immediate on-screen reflection.

docs.title: House leveling
docs.text:
Levels 1–4. Decoration slots equal the house level (1/2/3/4); upgrade costs are in Pricing (100 / 200 / 400, doubling per step, capped at level 4).

Per-level visuals — model swap (#59, Derek 2026-07-25). Leveling a house up swaps its City Kit Suburban mesh for the next rung of a per-house ladder, so a home visibly grows as it is upgraded. Each ladder is anchored on its Level-1 mesh — the level-1 entry is exactly the as-built mesh HouseStyleTable assigns that house, so a level-1 house renders identically to today. The approved L1→L4 ladders:

House L1 L2 L3 L4 1 building-type-r building-type-c building-type-s building-type-b 2 building-type-h building-type-i building-type-g building-type-f 3 building-type-k building-type-l building-type-j building-type-d 4 building-type-q building-type-e building-type-u building-type-n

A 5th ladder for zone-built houses (#299). Houses the player builds on zone lots (id ≥ 5) don't have a fixed per-house ladder — they roll one of five ladders (the four starter ladders above plus a 5th, HouseLevelModelTable id key 5, size-ordered L1→L4 building-type-o → building-type-p → building-type-a → building-type-m) and one of a generated 20-color tint palette, seeded deterministically on the house id and persisted across upgrades. Leveling still swaps the mesh up the rolled ladder exactly as it does for a starter. The full rule (assignment, persistence, palette generation, color-multiply tint) is in Art Style → House architecture and the #57 build note above.

All four levels render their chosen kit mesh (v0.6 de-graybox pass, Derek's directive "I want the house models we chose at all levels, not graybox"). Every rung of every ladder now has a full HouseModelCatalog entry, so an upgraded house shows its real City Kit Suburban mesh — never the graybox placeholder. Houses render at one fixed uniform kit scale (HousePlacement.KitScale, no per-model normalization), so a bigger mesh renders bigger: the size growth is real, and every ladder mesh's footprint still fits the shared lot envelope the starters already occupy at that scale, so leveling never resizes or moves the lot — its quadrant bounds and hand-picked centre are untouched. The house visual on that lot does re-align each level, though (#454): a taller/deeper upgrade mesh has a different footprint depth, so its front-setback pivot, its HousePlacement.HouseFootprint rect, and the front walkway that meets its door are all resolved from the house's current level's model (HouseModelCatalog.ForHouse(houseId, level), threaded through HousePlacement.Position/PositionFor/HouseFootprint), keeping the upgraded facade exactly FrontSetback from the sidewalk instead of drifting off the level-1 calibration. HouseUpgradeDirector.RefreshHouse re-aligns all three together — it rebuilds the mesh at the level-aware pivot and calls WalkNetwork.RefreshFrontWalkway(lot, level) so mesh, visible door, and walkway agree at the new level. (The earlier note that placement was resolved from the level-1 mesh regardless of level — the ZoneHousePlacementLevel shortcut — held only for the level-blind HouseModelCatalog.ForHouse(houseId) overload, still used where no level is in hand.) Core carries only mesh-name strings (Doggiehood.Core.Art.HouseLevelModelTable); the geometry lives in HouseModelCatalog. The only thing still deferred is the front-door anchor of each non-L1 ladder mesh (and the r/h/q L1 starters): those are provisional placeholders (centered on X, z = −FootprintZ/4, strictly inside the footprint) pending a gallery authoring pass — the models themselves are final, and the walkway re-aligns to whatever anchor each level's model carries (provisional or final). The graybox fallback still exists, but is now reached only when the kit model can't load or a house carries no resolvable ladder (a zone house with no rolled variant, or an unknown expansion id) — since #299, an ordinary zone-built house resolves its rolled ladder and renders a real kit mesh.

Decoration capacity = house level. A yard holds at most as many decorations as its level (1/2/3/4); a placement past capacity is rejected. See Decorations for the cap and its grandfathering rule (yards that already held more than their level's cap when this shipped keep everything — the cap blocks new placements only).

Implementation note (#59): GameState.TryUpgradeHouse(houseId) is the one Core entry point — it charges Doggiehood.Core.Expansion.HouseUpgradeNumbers.CostToReach (100/200/400) from Wallet and raises the house's level (House.RaiseLevel), returning false with no state change when the house is unknown, already at HouseUpgradeNumbers.MaxLevel (4), or unaffordable. The decoration cap is GameState.TryAddDecoration (capacity = level); the raw AddDecoration stays uncapped so save-load and grandfathered data are never removed. The player-facing upgrade button ships on the house profile view (#294): its footer Upgrade button calls TryUpgradeHouse directly on tap (Derek's Option A — no confirmation screen), shows the next step's cost, disables into a Max level state at the cap, and greys out when the live wallet can't afford the next step (HouseProfile.CanAffordUpgrade). The mesh-swap is a world re-render on the Unity side (#407): WorldBuilder.BuildHouse picks the mesh by level once, at build time, so raising the level in Core does not by itself grow the already-built HouseView — a v0.6 playtest bug left the world house on its old mesh while only the profile panel advanced. On a successful TryUpgradeHouse the overlay's upgrade wiring now asks HouseUpgradeDirector.RefreshHouse to destroy the stale HouseView and rebuild it through BuildHouse at the new level (the mirror of how ExpansionDirector swaps an empty-lot marker for the real house on build), then re-wires the fresh view's taps to both the profile-open handler and QuestDirector's spray path (via the idempotent QuestDirector.WireHouses) so a rebuilt house stays tappable. Rebuilding from the same Core House/HouseLot preserves a zone house's rolled ladder + palette tint (#299) and a vacant house's greyscale (#58). Because the live quest-delivery flow (QuestManager.DeliverPackage) still uses the uncapped AddDecoration, the capacity cap governs the new TryAddDecoration path only — how a decoration quest behaves against a full yard is a separate, undesigned decision left for when the decoration/upgrade UI is built.

docs.title: Expansion indicator (discoverability)
docs.text:
The neighborhood needs a visible signal that it can grow — a marker on the map for an unexplored/expandable zone, tinted so the player can tell at a glance whether they can afford to unlock it right now. Where the unlock action lives is now settled (Derek, 2026-07-28, on #343): the lock icon itself is the affordance (Option A) — tapping an affordable (gold) lock raises the reusable confirmation dialog, and Yes unlocks the zone. The remaining onboarding piece of #178 (how the player first learns coins unlock zones) stays a separate, open discoverability question; this section covers the indicator and its tap.

Decisions (Derek, on #178): the indicator is a lock icon marking the locked/expandable zone (2026-07-16) — Kenney's locked Game Icon (CC0), staged at Assets/Art/UI/ExpansionIndicator/Resources/locked.png. It hovers just past the end of the road at the entrance to the next locked zone (2026-07-18: "The icon could be hovering just passed the end of the road"), with its position derived from the zone's authored tile layout (#109) rather than hand-placed. It tints gold when the wallet covers the next zone's unlock cost, grey/black otherwise (2026-07-18: "Grey or black lock icon if can't purchase. Gold icon if affordable."), updating live as the balance changes. Since #343 the tint also gates the tap: tapping a gold lock raises the confirmation dialog, a grey/black lock's tap is a no-op — what the tint promises is exactly what the tap does. The one remaining #178 question (onboarding the coins→zones concept) stays open.

Implementation note (#178, reworked by #453, corrected by #537): Doggiehood.Core.Expansion.ExpansionIndicatorPlacement.Resolve(placed, frontierCoordinate, frontierType) finds the frontier coordinate's shared edge that actually carries a road into the placed TileMap — a road on both sides of the edge, the same TileMap.HasRoadConnectionAt predicate that gates the frontier, not merely any bordering edge — then returns that road edge's midpoint (TileGeometry.EdgeMidpoint) pushed ExpansionIndicatorNumbers.HoverOffset (one WorldDimensions.RoadWidth) further away from the map — "just past the end of the road". A lock therefore always anchors to an open road edge, never a grass/non-road neighbour edge (#537, Derek: "Locks should always be on the edge of roads, nothing else"); the frontier tile's type comes from GameState.TargetMap. If no shared edge carries a road it throws — impossible for a real TileFrontier-sourced coordinate, which is already road-connection-gated. Doggiehood.Core.Expansion.ExpansionIndicator.ResolveAll(state) returns one (TileCoordinate, ExpansionIndicatorState) entry per coordinate in GameState.UnlockableFrontier(), each priced/tinted via the #295 pricing path (TileUnlock.Cost vs the live wallet), NOT ZoneUnlock. On the Unity side, ExpansionUnlockDirector (via WorldBuilder.SyncExpansionIndicators) builds and maintains one ExpansionIndicatorView per unlockable frontier coordinate (spawn for a newly-open coordinate, destroy for one that got placed), each re-reading its own live state every frame — the same "never cache" contract the HUD currency chip uses for the wallet — and hiding itself once its coordinate leaves the frontier. This supersedes the retired single fixed marker (ExpansionIndicator.Resolve(state) / ExpansionIndicatorPlacement.Resolve(map, zone)), which is deleted. The staged icon is a literal black silhouette (RGB (0,0,0), shape carried in alpha), which a standard multiply tint can never recolor (black × anything is still black); Doggiehood.Unity.TintedIcon.Recolor instead builds a new texture preserving the source alpha but replacing every pixel's RGB with the target tint (Palette.ExpansionIndicatorAffordableHex / Palette.ExpansionIndicatorLockedHex), and the view swaps between two precomputed sprites rather than re-tinting every frame. The icon's .meta pins isReadable: 1 (Read/Write Enabled) so GetPixels32 can read it at runtime, per Hand-Authoring Unity Serialized Assets.

Implementation note (#343, reworked by #453) — the tap-to-unlock trigger. The affordability/cost decision is Core: an indicator's ExpansionIndicatorState (from ExpansionIndicator.ResolveAll) carries the flat TileUnlock.Cost and whether the live wallet affords it, the source the dialog reads (the retired ZoneUnlockOffer is deleted). On the Unity side each per-coordinate ExpansionIndicatorView is tappable (IInteractable + a BoxCollider sized to the sprite, toggled off with the renderer so a hidden lock isn't tappable): tapping an affordable lock raises UnlockRequested with its own coordinate, gated by the same live affordability + frontier-membership that tints/shows it — a grey or stale lock's tap does nothing. ExpansionUnlockDirector wires that event to the reusable ConfirmationDialog (built to confirmation-dialog.md, device-safe UGUI via CandyChromeUgui/bundled font, #298/#291) showing that tile's cost on Yes; Yes calls GameState.TryUnlockTile(coordinate), then the newly unlocked tile is rendered as real neighborhood (WorldBuilder.RenderUnlockedTile; see the #373 note below), its empty-lot markers wired to the #57 build path via ExpansionDirector.WireLots, the lock set is reconciled (that coordinate's lock disappears; any newly-open frontier locks appear), and the world is saved — mirroring how #57 wires EmptyLotView → TryBuildHouse. The currency HUD reflects the spend automatically (it reads Wallet.Coins live).

Implementation note (#373) — the unlocked zone renders as real neighborhood. A v0.6-playtest bug left a newly unlocked zone as bare lot markers floating over void — no grass, no roads — and the camera couldn't pan far enough to reach it. Both gaps are fixed by deriving the world's ground and roads from the live GameState.Map rather than the fixed starting geometry:
