docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Entry-point gear rendering (#370). The HUD gear (the entry point, drawn by HudOverlay, not the panel) wears the shared Candy Cottage chrome, matching the neighbouring currency chip: an Ink outline disc with a hard straight-down drop-shadow over a cream fill, and a procedural Ink toothed-disc gear icon — no font glyph, no raster art. It previously drew a ⚙ (U+2699) font glyph on a default IMGUI button, which the bundled DejaVuSans cannot render, so on device it fell back to an unstyled gray box (#291). Placement (GearButtonSizePx = 88, GearMarginPx = 32) and behaviour (tap opens Settings) are unchanged; see hud.md.
  • Debug unlock gesture. Tapping the version label 10 times within 10 seconds reveals the Debug tab in the sidebar; fewer taps, or 10 spread over more than 10s, does not. The gesture + the debug-toggle registry are engine-free Core logic (unit-tested); the panel/tabs/version display/toggle wiring is the Unity layer (#219).
  • Debug ships hidden. The Debug menu is in the build but unreachable without the gesture — no stray entry point.
  • The Debug tab is in shipping builds on purpose, for now (#656, Derek). Every Debug affordance — including the Tune balance… row and the tuning menu it opens — is built in every build (development, release-candidate and the shipping release alike), with the 10-tap unlock as its only gate. No Debug row carries a build-configuration gate on top of it; #622's dev-build-only rule for the tuning row was reversed by #656. This is deliberate and temporary: the debug menu stays in the game while the balance is still being dialed in on-device, and the entire debug menu (tab, gesture, rows, tuning panel) is removed in one later pass once Derek and Lucas are comfortable with the game — that removal gets its own issue at that time. Because the gesture is the only gate, it is asserted directly by EditMode tests rather than assumed.
  • Bundled UI font. This is the game's first runtime-built UGUI (the HUD/onboarding are IMGUI), so its shader and font must be pulled into the build explicitly or the Android build strips them — the panel rendered as a magenta box with invisible text on device (#291). Fixed by retaining UI/Default in Always Included Shaders and bundling DejaVu Sans (Assets/UI/Fonts/Resources/DejaVuSans.ttf — deliberately outside the Assets/Art low-poly-scanned tree, loaded via Resources.Load) instead of the Editor-only Resources.GetBuiltinResource lookup. DejaVu covers the ✕ close glyph but not the fullwidth plus, so the Add coins action uses a plain ASCII +. See docs/engineering/unity-serialization.md.
  • Runtime UGUI input needs an EventSystem. UGUI pointer input requires both a GraphicRaycaster on the canvas (owned by UiCanvas) and an active EventSystem with an input module in the scene. Unity only auto-creates an EventSystem from the Editor's menu, never for runtime-built UI, so without one every control in this panel (close ✕, version-tap unlock, scrim tap-to-close, Debug toggles) is inert on device even though the handlers are wired — while the IMGUI HUD gear still opens Settings because it bypasses the EventSystem (#327). WorldBootstrap therefore ensures exactly one persistent EventSystem + StandaloneInputModule beside the UiCanvas (the classic legacy-input module, matching activeInputHandler: 0), guarded against duplicates in UiEventSystem.Ensure().
  • Standard this sets. New debug affordances live as toggles/actions in this Debug tab, not as temporary code edits (#219).
  • Future tabs (audio, save/reset) are out of scope, but the sidebar leaves room for them.
  • Reference resolution. Constants are authored at the 1920×1200 (16:10) reference per Overview; a Unity CanvasScaler scales from this so each px constant has a fixed meaning across tablet sizes.
  • Style itself (outlines, flat shadows, pill shapes, rounded type) lives in Art & UI Style; this page is layout only.

docs.title: Design decisions (resolved)
docs.text:
1. Entry point — how Settings opens → a gear button in the HUD's top-right corner (furthest right), with the currency chip moved just inboard, to the gear's left. This nudges the currency-chip placement, so the HUD wireframe (#174) is flagged to reconcile — the gear takes the corner.
  2. Sidebar vs. bottom tabs on portrait → sidebar only. The game is landscape-locked (#22/#256), so there is no portrait case that would need a bottom-tab variant.
  3. Does the Debug unlock persist across launches? → resets each session (ships hidden, re-hidden every launch; re-tap to reveal). Persisting across launches remains a one-flag change if we later prefer it.

docs.title: Shared UI Components
docs.text:
Wireframe issue: #173 (stub established in #172). Style source: Art & UI Style (#65). Mockup: mockups/shared-components.html.

Reference resolution: 1920×1200 (16:10 tablet, landscape — #22). Every layout constant on this page is authored against that reference; a Unity CanvasScaler scales from it. See the target platform note.

Atomic, reusable UI pieces are documented once, here, and referenced by every per-screen wireframe that uses them — never re-specified per screen. This page is the shared reference: a screen's page names a component and points here, rather than restating its shape, outline, or shadow.

The style of every component below comes from the "Candy Cottage" direction settled in Art & UI Style. This page pulls the rules that apply to every component forward as the shared baseline; the full rationale and the reference mockup live on that page. What this page adds on top of style is layout: each component's regions and its named layout constants (per #161), which implementation declares and EditMode tests assert against.

docs.title: Shared style baseline (Candy Cottage)
docs.text:
Every UI component inherits, from Art & UI Style:

  • Thick dark outlines on all chrome.
  • Flat, hard drop-shadows — no blur.
  • Chunky pill / rounded shapes — pill-shaped buttons and chips.
  • Bold rounded sans-serif type.

A sticker-book feel, chosen for legibility against the bright/saturated palette and low-poly toy-shelf look.

docs.title: Shared baseline constants
docs.text:
Inherited by every component; a component's own table adds only what is specific to it.

Constant Value Applies to OutlineThicknessPx 6 dark outline on all chrome ShadowOffsetPx 8 hard drop-shadow, straight down, no blur PillRadiusPx 999 buttons & chips (full pill) PanelRadiusPx 40 dialogue box / panel chrome

These baseline constants + the palette below are realized in code from this single source (no per-screen hand-picked values, #161): the IMGUI overlays draw them via CandyChrome (HUD chip #296, onboarding), and the retained-UGUI panels via CandyChromeUgui (Settings #298) — both procedural, no raster art asset.

docs.title: Outline: a constant-width contour band (#616)
docs.text:
The dark outline is a constant-width contour band of width OutlineThicknessPx that follows the fill's rounded-rect contour exactly — the same even thickness on straight edges and around every corner. It is not the offset-copy Outline mesh effect (four diagonally-shifted stamps of the graphic), whose union is not constant-width around a curve — it bulges on-axis and thins/dips off-axis, the uneven look reported in #616. Both chrome helpers realize the band the same way: the same procedural rounded sprite, inflated by the band width (extents and corner radius each grow by W), drawn behind the fill — so a uniform W of Ink shows around the whole perimeter and the fill's own contour is the band's inner edge by construction (fill radius and outline inner radius can never drift).

Acceptance test (border-evenness invariant). Chrome outline evenness is a checkable pixel-level spec, not an eyeballed one. Ray-marching outward from a rendered element's centre through densely-sampled angles (through each corner arc): the fill→ink transition traces a true rounded-rect contour (a round corner arc, no inward dip), and the perpendicular ink-band width is constant within an anti-aliasing tolerance (±1px) across all angles, corners included. The geometry is proved engine-free in Doggiehood.Core.Ui.RoundedRectContour; the Unity EditMode pixel test enforces it against the actually-baked chrome with two complementary instruments: (1) the ray-march checker measures the band on the baked alpha across each corner's curved span, marching along the analytic contour normal (a 9-slice bake's straight strips reach the clamped texture border, so near-axis texels cannot be cleanly sampled bilinearly); and (2) a per-texel bake-fidelity assertion pins every texel of the baked texture — border-hugging near-axis arc texels included — to the analytic contour coverage (RoundedRectContour.Coverage), which transfers the engine-free constant-band proof to the bake at all angles with no sampling involved.

Regions: label (optional leading icon) inside a single pill; role tint applied to the fill.

Constant Value Region HeightPx 96 tap target PaddingXPx 48 label inset FontSizePx 36 label IconGapPx 16 icon → label

docs.title: Currency chip (CurrencyChip)
docs.text:
The HUD coin indicator — a coin token plus the live balance. Sits in a screen corner (its anchor is fixed in the HUD wireframe, #174).

Status: implemented in the HUD (#296) — Assets/Scripts/Unity/HudOverlay.cs draws the cream pill, Ink outline, hard drop-shadow, and gold coin token to the constants below; the balance is the bare tabular number (the coin token supplies the "coins" meaning). Sized to match the Settings gear beside it (#440): the chip height equals GearButtonSizePx (88) and the interior is scaled ×1.375 to fill the taller pill.

Regions: coin token (left) · balance number (right, tabular figures) · floating delta label (transient, appears below the chip on a balance change), inside a cream pill.

Constant Value Region HeightPx 88 chip (matches the Settings gear) CoinDiameterPx 60 coin token PaddingLeftPx 14 coin inset PaddingRightPx 36 number inset FontSizePx 46 balance (tabular) DeltaFontSizePx 32 delta label text DeltaOffsetYPx 12 gap: chip bottom edge → delta label start DeltaRiseDistancePx 48 total rise distance before the label is discarded DeltaRiseDurationSec 0.9 delta rise + fade duration CountUpDurationSec 0.5 balance-number count-up (tween) duration

Balance-change animation (#542). On a Wallet.Coins change the chip spawns a delta label showing the signed amount — +123 in Leaf (the palette's positive/confirm role) on a gain, −45 in Coral (primary/spend) on a spend — starting DeltaOffsetYPx below the chip and centred under it. It rises DeltaRiseDistancePx while fading linearly to transparent over DeltaRiseDurationSec, then is discarded (no new colors are introduced — the delta reuses the shared palette). Independently, the displayed balance counts up from its prior displayed value to the new live Wallet.Coins value over CountUpDurationSec rather than snapping; a second change before the count-up finishes just re-targets it toward the newer value (from wherever it currently reads) rather than queuing. Each change spawns its own delta-label instance — there is no stacking/queue model for the label (unlike the reward toast, #541, which carries the message; this chip carries only the running-total motion). Purely decorative: it does not register with ModalInputGate and never blocks a tap. The count-up + rise/fade math is Unity-independent (Doggiehood.Core.Economy.CoinChipAnimation, plain-NUnit tested); HudOverlay only reads it each frame and paints it.

docs.title: Modal overlays block world input
docs.text:
Every dialog/menu overlay is modal: a tap that lands on it — on a button, on the panel's empty area, or on its dimmed backdrop — is consumed by the UI and never reaches a world interactable (a dog, a house, a lost item) behind it (#422). Tapping Accept only accepts; tapping Close only closes; neither also fires whatever sat behind the button.

This is why every center-anchored overlay (confirmation dialog, house profile, dog profile) carries a full-screen raycast-blocking scrim/backdrop under its card. A new center-anchored modal surface must include such a backdrop, or taps on its empty regions would fall through to the world. The bottom-center conversation panel is the exception — it has no scrim (tapping outside it does not dim the world), so it can rely only on the shared registry below, not on a backdrop; the EventSystem.IsPointerOverGameObject check covers just its own button/panel rects, and until #568 it was not on the registry at all (a tap just outside its rects leaked to the world).

The world tap-router (see Camera & controls → Navigation) enforces the block two ways:

  • A shared modal registry (ModalInputGate, #544). Every modal surface — confirmation dialog, dog profile, house profile, welcome pop-up, onboarding reward, and the conversation panel (#568) — registers itself as open on show and unregisters on close (and again if it is destroyed while open, so a torn-down overlay never leaves the block set). While any is registered (IsBlocking) the tap-router swallows the tap before its world raycast. The registry also exposes a one-call reset used at hard boundaries — scene unload, or test isolation — so a stale registration can never leak past that boundary and leave world taps dead. This is a deterministic, frame-timing-independent flag: it is the authoritative guard, added because the original EventSystem.IsPointerOverGameObject signal alone could miss a fast touch tap-release over the scrim and leak that tap to the world object behind the panel (opening it and closing the profile).
  • A same-frame close latch (ClosedThisFrame / EndFrame(), #568). IsBlocking alone is a live snapshot of the open-token count, and a panel's Unregister runs synchronously while the EventSystem dispatches the very tap that dismissed it — but EventSystem.Update() and the camera rig's tap-routing Update() have no defined order. If the EventSystem runs first, IsBlocking already reads false for that same tap, which then falls through and fires whatever world object sat under the panel (the reported "one tap closes the window and opens the object underneath" bug). So Unregister of a still-open modal latches ClosedThisFrame, the tap-router blocks on IsBlocking || ClosedThisFrame, and CameraRig.LateUpdate calls EndFrame() to clear the latch — Unity runs every LateUpdate only after all Updates have completed, so the closing tap stays consumed for the rest of its frame regardless of ordering, while the next frame's genuinely-new tap routes normally. A no-op Unregister (unknown / already-removed / null token) does not latch, so a frame with no modal open never dead-ends a world tap.
  • EventSystem.IsPointerOverGameObject on the backdrop remains as a belt-and-suspenders check for overlays not (yet) on the registry.

Blocking suppresses only the world pass-through. A scrim/backdrop's own close/cancel button still fires through UGUI, so a panel that intentionally dismisses on scrim tap keeps doing so — "dismiss this panel" and "pass the tap through to the world" stay distinct.

The one still-IMGUI affordance, the HUD Settings gear, sits outside the EventSystem and so is covered by an interim screen-space rect guard instead; it folds into this same rule once it migrates to UGUI (#370).

docs.title: Toast notification
docs.text: Wireframe issue: #562. Implements/covers: ToastNotification. Approved: Derek, 2026-08-04 (/approve on #562) — authoritative layout contract. Mockup: mockups/toast.html. Status: implemented (#541) — the engine-free single-slot Doggiehood.Core.Ui.ToastQueue<T> sequences requests; Assets/Scripts/Unity/ToastView.cs renders the current slot in the reserved top-left lane (IMGUI HUD element, mirroring the currency chip); and the two directors (QuestCompletionDirector off QuestManager.QuestCompleted, OnboardingRewardDirector off OnboardingRewardChain.RewardGranted) assemble copy (ToastCopy) and enqueue. Wired in WorldBootstrap.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
A small, non-modal notification that slides into a reserved top-left lane to celebrate a completion the player just earned, then clears itself on a short auto-timeout (or the moment it is tapped). It is the standard "you did that, and here's your reward" surface for two — and only two — triggers: quest completion (QuestManager.Complete) and onboarding reward-chain step completion (OnboardingRewardChain.RewardGranted). It is a HUD element like the currency chip, not a centered panel: it never dims the world, never blocks input, and mirrors the chip's reservation in the opposite corner. Reference resolution is 1920×1200 per Overview.

Deliberately not a centered modal. It replaces the modal-per-step onboarding reward panel for the reward-chain's completion feedback (reversing the #374 "brief modal celebration beat" exception — see Notes) with a lightweight toast that never interrupts play, while still sitting on the shared Candy Cottage baseline and reusing the CurrencyChip coin token.

docs.title: Regions
docs.text: Region Contains Shared component Coin token A leading gold coin, reusing the CurrencyChip coin-token treatment — both triggers pay flat coins, so one icon covers both CurrencyChip coin token Message One short dynamic line: the accomplishment + payout, one sentence. The pill grows to the measured text width up to ToastMaxWidthPx; the line never wraps and never grows height (wordWrap off), and any message that would still exceed the cap is clipped at the pill edge (clipping = Clip) as a fail-safe rather than bleeding past it. ToastMaxWidthPx is sized so every currently-approved line fits on one line at ToastFontSizePx (#578) Reuses the Candy Cottage baseline (cream pill, thick outline, hard shadow) from Shared UI Components (no scrim, no button) The toast is the whole surface — no backdrop and no dedicated button; a tap anywhere on it dismisses early —

This page adds the toast-specific composition — the reserved lane, the single message line, the dismiss/queue timing — and sizes them.

docs.title: Per-toast copy — the two triggers
docs.text:
Both triggers render one line: the accomplishment sentence followed by the flat coin payout as "+N coins". The message is built in the thin Unity layer from Core-supplied data (the just-completed step/quest + amount); no copy lives in Core.

Trigger Copy Quest complete (any completion path, QuestManager.Complete) "Quest complete! +N coins" — N is the flat quest payout (economy.md, today 10) Onboarding — first quest "You finished your first quest! +100 coins" Onboarding — upgrade a house "You made a house even nicer! +100 coins" Onboarding — expand the map "You opened up a brand-new street! +100 coins" Onboarding — build a house "You built a brand-new house! +100 coins"

The four onboarding lines carry over verbatim from the retired onboarding reward panel's accepted per-step copy (/approve #374) — only the surface changes, not the words; the panel's separate "+N coins" button label folds into the one toast line. The onboarding amount is OnboardingRewardChainNumbers.RewardPerStep (100 today); the quest amount is the flat quest payout (10 today). Keep every line to one short sentence that fits on a single line within ToastMaxWidthPx at ToastFontSizePx — an EditMode guard measures every approved line against the pill's text budget so new copy (or a wider +N payout) that would overflow fails loudly instead of clipping the reward amount (#578).

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Not modal. Unlike every centered panel in shared components, the toast never registers with ModalInputGate and carries no backdrop — it is a HUD element like the currency chip, just tappable. World taps outside the reserved lane are unaffected; a tap on the toast only dismisses it and does not fall through to the world.
  • Dismiss model — both auto-timeout and tap. The toast clears itself after ToastAutoDismissSeconds, and a tap anywhere on it dismisses early; either path runs the same ToastSlideOutMs exit. It can never trap the player (the same anti-soft-lock posture as the confirmation dialog and #329).
  • Sequential queue, one slot (ToastQueueSlotCount = 1). Only one toast is ever visible. If a second trigger fires while one is showing — e.g. a quest-complete and an onboarding-reward toast landing close together — the second waits and plays immediately after the first's slide-out finishes, never stacked or overlapping. Order is first-come, first-served.
  • Reverses #374's modal exception (confirmed intended per #541's revise thread): the onboarding reward-chain step's completion feedback moves off the centered OnboardingRewardPanel (scrim + button) onto this toast. onboarding-reward.md and onboarding.md's reward-chain section are reconciled accordingly.
  • HUD reservation mirrors the chip. hud.md gains a Toast lane region, top-left, sized to ToastHeightPx + margins — nothing else renders there, the same posture as the CurrencyChip's reserved top-right region.
  • Payout stays in Core. The toast is pure presentation over the existing payout paths (QuestManager.Complete → Wallet.Deposit, OnboardingRewardChain → Wallet.Deposit); it shows the coins Core already granted and never moves coins itself. The currency chip updates on its own (it reads Wallet.Coins live). A reloaded chain never re-pays nor re-toasts.
  • Reference resolution. Constants are authored at the 1920×1200 (16:10) reference per Overview; a Unity CanvasScaler scales from this so each px constant has a fixed meaning across tablet sizes.
  • Style itself (outlines, flat shadows, pill shapes, rounded type, palette) lives in Art & UI Style; this page is layout only.

docs.title: Welcome pop-up
docs.text: Wireframe issue: #439. Implements/covers: WelcomePopup. Approved: Derek, 2026-07-31 (proposal + decisions, /approve on #439) — authoritative layout contract. Mockup: mockups/welcome-popup.html.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: A modal celebration panel — "Welcome to the neighborhood!" — raised when the move-in system fills a vacant house, announcing the new arrival(s) to the player. It reuses the onboarding reward panel composition (portrait medal overlapping the top edge, big heading, one leaf pill), just parameterized for an arrival instead of a coin payout, so a move-in reads as the same warm celebration beat. One pop-up per household. Its single "Say hi!" button pans the camera to the new house and opens that house's profile (#604) so the player lands on their new neighbour with the resident dog(s) one tap away. Reference resolution is 1920×1200 per Overview.

docs.title: Regions
docs.text: Region Contains Shared component Scrim Full-screen dim behind the panel; tapping it dismisses (same as the button) so the celebration is never a trap — Portrait badge A single round medal overlapping the panel's top edge, carrying the new dog's (household head's) portrait — a graybox dog silhouette now; a real tinted dog-model portrait is a fast-follow (see Notes) Reuses the Candy Cottage baseline (thick outline, hard shadow) from Shared UI Components Heading The fixed celebratory headline — "Welcome to the neighborhood!" Shared panel chrome Name The new dog's name, or the household's names for a multi-dog move-in (e.g. "Biscuit & Pepper") Shared panel chrome Meta One dynamic line: breed · household composition / which house (e.g. "French Bulldog · moved in next door", "French Bulldog family of 2", "moved in — 3 dogs") Shared panel chrome Member-chip row A row of small named portrait chips, one per dog in the household — the household head keeps the big portrait badge. Hidden entirely for a single-dog move-in. Reuses the chip shape baseline Action One positive/leaf pill button — "Say hi!" — which dismisses, pans the camera to the new house, and opens that house's profile (#604) PillButton

The panel chrome (outline OutlineThicknessPx = 6 / corner radius PanelRadiusPx = 40 / hard drop-shadow) and the Say hi! button (96 px PillButton) are owned by the shared components (#173) and not re-specified here — the same reference posture the onboarding reward panel takes. This page adds the welcome-specific composition — the portrait medal, the heading, the name, the meta, the member-chip row, and the button — and sizes them.

docs.title: Household variants
docs.text:
The move-in system produces households in a 70% single / 25% parent+puppy / 5% three-dog mix (Move-in system). There is one pop-up per household, never one per dog; the household head keeps the big portrait badge.

  • Single (70%) — the common case: one portrait badge, one name, one meta line. The member-chip row is hidden — a lone dog needs no chip echoing the portrait above it.
  • Parent + puppy (25%) — the household head's portrait in the badge; the name line reads both names (e.g. "Biscuit & Pepper"); the meta reads the shared breed and family size (e.g. "French Bulldog family of 2"). A member-chip row of two named chips appears below the meta, one per dog.
  • Three-dog (5%) — one pop-up for the whole household (not three), head's portrait in the badge, meta "moved in — 3 dogs", and a member-chip row of three named chips.

The hidden-for-single rule: the member-chip row renders only when the household has more than one dog. For single move-ins the panel collapses to portrait → heading → name → meta → button, with no empty row and no reserved gap.

docs.title: Timing
docs.text: The panel pops WelcomePopupDelaySeconds (range 1–3s, default 1.5s) after the previous panel closes — the move-in is triggered by a completed quest, and this delay keeps the welcome from stacking on top of the quest-resolution feedback that fired it. The move-in celebration is always its own clean beat, never overlaid on another panel. WelcomePopupDelaySeconds is a named, tunable constant like every value here.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• One pop-up per household, parameterized. The caller passes the household (head + members), their names, breed, and which house; the heading and chrome are constant. The card grows vertically with its content (name/meta wrap, member-chip row present or absent), exactly like the reward panel and confirmation card.
  • Always dismissible. The single Say hi! button dismisses; tapping the scrim also dismisses — the same anti-soft-lock posture as the reward panel and confirmation dialog. One button only — a welcome is an acknowledgement, not a choice.
  • The camera pan and profile-open are the non-presentational behaviors. Everything else on this panel is pure presentation, but "Say hi!" pans the camera to the new house via CameraController.FocusOn and opens that house's profile (#604) — so tapping it is truthful: the player is taken to meet their new neighbour, not just look at their roof, with the resident dog(s) one tap away. The profile-open reuses the exact same resolve a house tap uses (WorldBootstrap.OpenHouseProfile → HouseProfileOverlay.Open), so there is no duplicated lookup. The pan reuses the existing FocusOn and is a slightly wider scope than #373 chose for zone-unlock (which deliberately only let the player pan to a new zone). The welcome unregisters from the modal input gate on dismiss and the profile registers on open within the same synchronous Say hi! call, so exactly one modal stays registered across the hand-off and no world tap leaks in between (#544). Tapping the scrim dismisses without panning or opening anything.
  • Portrait is graybox now. The portrait badge and member chips show a graybox dog silhouette for now; a real tinted dog-model portrait — needs no new art, it renders the existing coat-tinted model — is a fast-follow, not part of this wireframe.
  • A brief celebration beat. Like the reward panel, this is a momentary modal (scrim + one button) the player taps through — a warm earned beat, not a tutorial screen. Move-ins are paced (gated behind a built vacant house), so a big earned beat fits.
  • Reference resolution. Constants are authored at the 1920×1200 (16:10) reference per Overview; a Unity CanvasScaler scales from this so each px constant has a fixed meaning across tablet sizes.
  • Style itself (outlines, flat shadows, pill shapes, rounded type, palette) lives in Art & UI Style; this page is layout only.

docs.title: UI Mockups
docs.text:
HTML mockups for approved wireframes live in this folder, one file per screen (<screen>.html), each corresponding 1:1 with its text spec under docs/specs/ui/. See the UI Design Process.

This folder is populated as wireframes are approved (epic #171).

docs.title: Mockups
docs.text:
• Shared UI Components — the shared reference (docs/specs/ui/shared-components.md) every per-screen wireframe points to.
  • HUD — HUD currency chip placement (#174).
  • Conversation Panel — the dialogue panel opened by tapping a dog's speech bubble (#175).
  • Onboarding Overlay — the first-launch bottom-center coach prompt (#176).
  • Dog Profile — the centered profile card opened by tapping a dog (#177).
  • Settings menu — sidebar tabs, About (version), and a hidden Debug tab (#218).
  • Onboarding reward panel — the bespoke celebration panel raised on completing each onboarding step (#374).
  • Welcome pop-up — the modal celebration panel raised when a new dog or household moves into a vacant house (#439).
  • Toast notification — the non-modal top-left toast for quest-completion and onboarding reward-chain step completion (#562).
  • Debug tuning menu — the utilitarian overlay of grouped balance sliders over the Core TuningConfig, reached from the Debug tab behind the 10-tap unlock (#621).

docs.title: Art & UI Style
docs.text:
Issues: #64 (world/house style), #65 (UI chrome)

The house and world palette below is implemented: the neighborhood renders real Kenney City Kit Suburban (CC0) models, staged under Assets/Art/Houses/CityKitSuburban/. The UI chrome direction ("Candy Cottage") is still a decided-but-not-yet-implemented spec for the components listed below.

docs.title: Color palette
docs.text:
Bright & saturated. Bold, punchy colors that read clearly at a distance and skew playful rather than naturalistic — not the muted/earthy or soft-pastel alternatives that were considered. (#64)

Environment surfaces (grass, street, sidewalk, crosswalk) carry this palette as hex constants on Doggiehood.Core.Art.Palette. Dog coats carry it as per-breed hex data. Houses carry it through the kit's own hand-painted textures (below), not through Core-owned hex color data.

docs.title: House architecture
docs.text:
Real kit models, one per house, painted with the kit's own texture variants. Each of the 4 starting houses (World & Neighborhood) renders as one of the 21 Kenney City Kit Suburban house meshes — chosen so no two starting houses share a model — giving each dog's home its own silhouette, rather than a uniform tract-house look. (#64)

Per-house color comes from swapping in one of the kit's own hand-painted texture variants (colormap — the kit's default — plus variation-a/variation-b/variation-c) as the model's main texture, rather than from procedural roof/porch geometry or Core-owned hex colors. Doggiehood.Core.Art.HouseStyleTable is the single source of truth for both which model (HouseStyle.ModelName) and which texture variant (HouseStyle.TintVariant) each starting house gets; WorldBuilder.BuildHouseModel applies the tint by cloning the model's renderer materials and setting .mainTexture to the loaded variant texture — a real texture swap, since the kit's variant textures are distinct hand-painted alternates, not a white base meant to be color-multiplied. The specific 4 model letters assigned are r/h/k/q: the Level-1 (as-built) mesh of each house's proposed #59 upgrade path, so homes start small and visibly grow as they level up. This is Derek's call (2026-07-25) resolving the earlier placeholder picks flagged in #122; each house keeps its original tint variant (the tint is independent of the model). The per-house front-door anchors for the new starters r/h/q are provisional placeholders (centered on X, toward the street) pending a gallery authoring pass, unlike the door data for the retained meshes, which is authored. Swapping which of the 21 letters is used is a config change to HouseStyleTable, not a rebuild.

Because r/h/k/q are each house's Level-1 mesh, upgrading a house (#59) swaps in the next rung of its per-house model ladder — the full L1→L4 ladders and their "anchored on L1" rule live in Neighborhood Expansion → House leveling, backed by Doggiehood.Core.Art.HouseLevelModelTable. As of the v0.6 de-graybox pass every rung has a full HouseModelCatalog entry, so all four levels render their chosen kit mesh at the fixed uniform HousePlacement.KitScale — a house visibly grows as it levels up while every ladder mesh still fits the shared lot envelope (no per-model normalization, no lot resize). The only thing still deferred is the door anchor of each non-L1 ladder mesh (and the r/h/q L1 starters), which stays a provisional placeholder pending a gallery authoring pass; the models are final. The graybox fallback remains only for a genuinely-unknown mesh (e.g. an expansion house with no ladder).

Zone-built houses get a rolled look, not a fixed one (#299). The 4 starters above have hand-picked ladders and tints; every house the player builds on an unlocked zone lot (id ≥ 5) instead rolls its own — one of five model ladders and one of a generated 20-color palette of tints — settled by Derek (2026-07-28). The roll happens when the zone unlocks (the lot first appears), not lazily at build time (#434, moving #299's original build-time timing earlier), so the empty lot already knows the house that will stand on it — driving its house-sized foundation footprint and pre-placed yard trees (see the #57 build note). The five ladders are the four starter ladders plus a new 5th ladder (HouseLevelModelTable id key 5, size-ordered L1→L4 o → p → a → m, all catalogued via #348). The pick is a deterministic seeded RNG keyed on the house id (Doggiehood.Core.Art.HouseVariantAssignment), so it's stable across sessions and iteration order, assigned once at GameState.TryUnlockNextZone (stored in GameState.AssignedLotVariants; TryBuildHouse reads that pre-assignment, falling back to the deterministic HouseVariantAssignment.ForHouse roll for a legacy save with no persisted entry) and persisted (ladder id + tint index) through SaveCodec — a lotvariant= line for an assigned-but-unbuilt lot, or the house= line once built — so it survives relaunch and the house's L1→L4 upgrades — leveling swaps the mesh within the rolled ladder, never re-rolls. The tint palette is a curated, hand-picked 20-entry list (Palette.HouseTintHex), settled by Derek & Lucas (2026-08-02, #519) after an earlier generated even-18°-hue / fixed S = 0.70, V = 0.90 rule produced an unpleasant electric violet/blue: 10 slots are kept from those generated values and the 10 flagged (electric) ones are softened — mostly desaturated, with the cool blues/violets nudged lighter. It stays index-stable at 20 entries, and each house stores its tint index (0–19), so the retune re-colors every existing house onto the approved palette for free with no save migration. Unlike the starters' .mainTexture variant swap, the tint is applied as a material color-multiply over the mesh (the same ApplyVacancyTint technique, via WorldBuilder.ApplyPaletteTint) — and the vacancy grey (#58) still wins while the house is vacant, with the palette color showing on move-in.

The placement, footprint, and fence call sites resolve a zone house through that same rolled ladder (#414). HouseModelCatalog.ForHouse(houseId) is the one zone-aware chokepoint: for a starter id (1–4) it resolves via HouseStyleTable as before, and for a zone id (≥ 5) it returns the rolled ladder's level-1 mesh (HouseVariantAssignment → HouseLevelModelTable.ForHouseLevel(ladderId, 1) → ForModel) instead of throwing through HouseStyleTable.ForHouse. That keeps HousePlacement.HouseFootprint/Position, LotFence, and the yard/quest placement that reuses the footprint zone-safe once a zone lot has a front walkway — which it does once WalkNetwork spans zone tiles (#398). These call sites carry only a HouseLot (no house.Level), and leveling never resizes or moves the lot (every ladder mesh fits the shared lot envelope), so the fixed level-1 footprint is a valid, level-invariant placement input; the rendered visual level is resolved separately from house.Level in WorldBuilder.BuildHouse.

When the kit model can't be loaded (an EditMode test seam, WorldBuilder.ForcePrimitiveFallback), houses fall back to a single plain graybox primitive with no per-house color or roof/porch detail — the graybox path exists to keep the world buildable/testable without the art assets, not to preserve the style spec on its own. A zone house with no rolled variant (an unknown expansion id, or one constructed directly in a test) likewise falls back to graybox.

docs.title: Delivery trucks
docs.text:
Trucks carry standard car colors, assigned per-spawn (#601). A delivery truck renders the single Kenney Car Kit "delivery" mesh, tinted with one of a small curated real-world car spread — white, black, silver, gray, red, dark blue, dark green (Palette.CarColorHex, settled by Derek 2026-08-05) — so trucks aren't all identical. This is deliberately not the broad decorative 20-tint house table (Palette.HouseTintHex); it's the tight, believable spread of colors actual cars come in. The tint is applied the same way houses are — a material color-multiply over the model's renderers (DeliveryTruckView mirroring WorldBuilder.ApplyPaletteTint).

Unlike a house — whose tint is a deterministic per-id roll (HouseVariantAssignment.ForHouse) that SaveCodec persists — a truck is transient and never saved, so its color is picked at spawn from an incrementing spawn seed (Doggiehood.Core.Art.CarColorAssignment, a pure function of that seed so it stays unit-testable), and the pick avoids the colors currently on the road so two concurrent trucks don't look alike. Nothing about a truck's color survives its trip off-map; each new truck rolls fresh.

docs.title: UI chrome direction: "Candy Cottage"
docs.text:
This section owns UI style only. UI layout — a screen's regions, anchors, and named size/margin constants — lives in the UI Wireframes section and follows the UI Design Process (wireframe approved before any code). The style rules below are pulled forward as the shared baseline on Shared UI Components; every per-screen wireframe references them rather than restating them.

Thick dark outlines on all UI chrome, flat hard drop-shadows (no blur), chunky pill-shaped buttons and chips, bold rounded sans-serif type. A sticker-book feel, chosen specifically over a flatter "paper-craft" alternative for its legibility and match with the bright/saturated palette and low-poly toy-shelf look. (#65)

The "thick dark outline" is a true constant-width contour stroke — an even band that follows the rounded contour around every corner — not an offset-copy approximation, whose four shifted stamps read as uneven/flattened corners. See the constant-width contour band on Shared UI Components (#616).

Applies to: the currency chip, the speech bubble indicator, the dialogue box, decoration/gift choice buttons, and should extend to menus/settings for consistency.

A reference mockup exists at this artifact, showing both the chosen "Candy Cottage" direction and the rejected "Flat Paper-Craft" alternative for contrast.

docs.title: Build checklist
docs.text:
• [x] Defined color palette (bright/saturated hex values, or the kit's equivalent hand-painted textures for houses) applied consistently across houses, dogs, UI
  • [x] 4 distinct house silhouettes (real kit models, one per house, painted with a distinct kit texture variant per house — the Level-1 mesh r/h/k/q of each house's #59 upgrade path, per Derek's 2026-07-25 call resolving the #122 placeholder picks; r/h/q door anchors provisional pending a gallery pass)
  • [x] Zone-built houses (id ≥ 5) render a real kit model — a deterministic rolled ladder (one of five) plus a curated-palette color-multiply tint (one of 20), assigned once and persisted across upgrades (#299) — instead of the graybox box
  • [x] Delivery trucks render the Car Kit mesh tinted with a curated standard car color (Palette.CarColorHex) picked per-spawn and kept distinct between concurrent trucks — a material color-multiply, not persisted like a house tint (#601)
  • [ ] UI components (buttons, chips, dialogue box) use thick dark outlines + flat hard drop-shadows (in progress: the HUD currency chip lands the full chrome — thick Ink outline + hard drop-shadow — in #296; the confirmation dialog #343, the conversation dialogue box + action/choice buttons #408, and the house profile + dog profile #465 now carry it; remaining screens' buttons still to come)
  • [ ] Currency chip, speech bubble icon, dialogue box, and choice buttons all follow the Candy Cottage direction (currency chip done — #296; dialogue box and choice buttons done — #408; the house/dog profiles done — #465; speech bubble icon remains)
  • [x] Menus/settings screens follow the same UI chrome for consistency (the Settings panel lands the full Candy Cottage chrome — thick Ink outlines, flat hard drop-shadows, rounded panel + pill tabs/close/action and the shared palette — in #298, via the UGUI CandyChromeUgui helper)

docs.title: Camera, Navigation & Controls
docs.text: Epic: #14

docs.title: No player character
docs.text: There is no visible player-controlled character in the world. The player is an unseen observer viewing the neighborhood from above and interacting with it directly — tapping dogs, houses, and items rather than moving an avatar. (#19)

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text:
Drag/swipe to pan the camera across the neighborhood; pinch to zoom in and out — the same interaction model as panning around a map. Tapping a dog or house triggers its interaction directly. (#20)

A tap over UI never reaches the world behind it. World tap-routing is modal-aware: when an open dialog/menu sits under the pointer, the tap is absorbed by that UI and the world raycast is skipped — so tapping Accept on a quest never also opens a house behind the button, and tapping Close never re-triggers the thing it sits over (#422). The authoritative guard is the shared modal registry (ModalInputGate) every modal surface registers with on open — including the scrim-less bottom-center conversation panel since #568, whose same-frame close latch also stops the dismissing tap itself from leaking to the world (see Shared components → Modal overlays block world input for the full mechanism). Belt-and-suspenders, the router also bails before any world hit-test when the tap is over a UGUI graphic (EventSystem.IsPointerOverGameObject, mouse and touch-fingerId overloads — the center-anchored overlays carry a full-screen raycast-blocking scrim, so this reads true anywhere over them) or over the still-IMGUI HUD Settings gear (a screen-space rect check against HudOverlay.ComputeGearRect, interim until the gear migrates to UGUI in #370).

The pan bounds grow with the map. Panning is clamped to the neighborhood's extent, but that extent is not fixed: it is derived from the live tile map (Doggiehood.Core.World.MapExtent.Covering — a named margin beyond the outermost tiles) and recomputes when a zone is unlocked (CameraController.RecomputeBoundsFromMap), so the player can always pan over to reach a newly unlocked zone rather than being clamped out of it (#373). The starting bounds derive from the same map-based path (the seeded origin tile), so there is one derivation for both the initial world and every expansion.

The maximum zoom-out grows with the map too. The minimum zoom-in and the default zoom are fixed, but the max zoom-out is not: it is re-derived from the same live map extent alongside the pan bounds, in the same CameraController.RecomputeBoundsFromMap recompute (a named padding beyond the outermost tiles so the map isn't framed edge-to-edge). So as the neighborhood spreads out with each expansion the player can always zoom out far enough to take the whole current map in at once, rather than hitting a fixed cap. Whenever the range recomputes, the current zoom is re-clamped into it — mirroring how the position is re-clamped — so an unlock never leaves the camera zoomed out past the new cap (#510). The grass ground plane is no longer sized to this max-zoom-out reach: #536 padded CameraController.GroundExtentForMap out to MaxZoom so the far zoom-out never framed past the grass, but because MaxZoom grows with the map the plane ballooned to dwarf the neighborhood (#558). The ground now pads only by the constant CameraController.BoundsMargin, and the "never frame past the grass" guarantee moves to a grass-coloured camera clear colour (CameraRig.ApplyConfiguration sets clearFlags = SolidColor, backgroundColor = Palette.GrassHex) — so however far the camera zooms out, any pixels beyond the mesh edge read as grass rather than the old blue void seam.

docs.title: Camera angle
docs.text:
Isometric / angled top-down camera — in the spirit of SimCity or Animal Crossing — rather than a straight bird's-eye view or a full free-orbit 3D camera. This shows house facades and roofs and keeps dogs easy to spot and tap. (#21)

The pitch (45°) and the orthographic projection are fixed. The yaw rotates freely, driven by a two-finger twist gesture: the neighborhood follows your fingers — twisting clockwise turns the scene clockwise (the camera itself yaws the opposite way), the same "content follows the finger" convention as drag-to-pan. Rotation is continuous — it does not snap to fixed angles and is not clamped to a range. This reopens the original "no free rotation/orbit" decision of #21 for yaw only, while keeping the recognisable angled-down look. (#203)

Note: the rotation control (#203) initially left the fixed-angle scene-visibility assumption in place — that content only ever needed to read well at the single fixed yaw. Camera-facing world markers now track the live camera yaw so they stay head-on at every rotation: speech bubbles and the map-expansion lock icon share one Core seam (CameraFacing.Resolve(cameraYaw) — fixed orthographic pitch, live yaw, zero roll) that the Unity layer re-applies each frame (#266). Broader scene content that is only authored for the fixed angle (e.g. facade-only art) is a separate follow-on, not covered by the marker-facing work.

docs.title: Orientation
docs.text:
The app is locked to landscape orientation — it never rotates to portrait — to better show off the neighborhood scene at once. (#22)

This is one facet of the project's platform target, stated authoritatively once — tablet, landscape, and the 1920×1200 (16:10) UI reference resolution — under UI Wireframes → Target platform & reference resolution. It is enforced in Unity by allowing only the two landscape orientations (portrait disabled, so the tablet auto-rotates between landscape-left and landscape-right but never to portrait) and scaling the UI canvas from that reference with a CanvasScaler (#256).

docs.title: Build checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Fixed pitch (45°) and orthographic projection, with free twist-driven yaw rotation (continuous, no snapping/clamping)
  • [ ] Camera-facing world markers (speech bubbles, map-expansion lock icon) track the live camera yaw and read head-on at every rotation (#266); broader fixed-angle scene-art readability remains a follow-on
  • [ ] Pan via drag/swipe within the bounds of the current neighborhood scene (the bounds grow with the map, recomputed from the live tile extent on zone unlock — #373)
  • [ ] Pinch-to-zoom with a fixed min zoom-in and a max zoom-out that grows with the live map extent (recomputed from the tile extent on zone unlock, mirroring the pan bounds — #510); the current zoom is re-clamped into the new range on each recompute
  • [ ] Tap-to-interact hit-testing on dogs and houses works at all zoom levels
  • [ ] A tap over an open dialog/menu (or its scrim, or the HUD gear) is absorbed by that UI and never reaches a world interactable behind it (#422)
  • [ ] App is locked to landscape orientation
  • [ ] No player avatar/character exists anywhere in the scene

docs.title: Sidewalks & Walk Network
docs.text: Related: #106 (this page), #105 (locked world dimensions this page consumes), #128 (front walkways, which replaced the driveway stubs on this page), #109 (multi-tile grid the walk network now derives its roads from, via #398), #112 (approach-to-rest movement, which routes dogs to their comfort decorations over this network)

docs.title: Symmetric sidewalk placement
docs.text:
Every road gets a sidewalk on both sides — not just one edge. Moving outward from the road centerline: road → verge setback → sidewalk, mirrored on the other side, with grass outside the sidewalk. The widths are the locked standard dimensions (WorldDimensions, #105) — nothing on this page introduces a new measurement:

Standard Value Road width 6m Grass verge (road edge → sidewalk) 0.75m — a logical setback, see below Sidewalk width 2m

Decision (2026-07-13, Derek, in conversation): the grass verge between road and sidewalk no longer exists — GrassVergeWidth went from 1.5m to 0m. This supersedes the original #106 verge. Context: aligning Core's walk geometry with the Kenney City Kit Roads art (#121/#122). At tile scale 10, a kit road tile has road surface 0–3m from the centerline and a raised curb+sidewalk band spanning 3–5m; with a 0m verge, Core's sidewalk centerline lands at exactly 4m — dogs walk centered on the kit's modeled pavement, and the crosswalk edges (±4m) land inside the crossroad tile's own corner sidewalks (4–5m). The constant stays in WorldDimensions (and in the offset formula) so the geometry keeps deriving from one place.

Decision (2026-07-13, Derek, in conversation — follow-up to the above, same day): GrassVergeWidth is now 0.75m. After seeing the kit world in the Editor, Derek found the dogs at 4m "a little too close to the road" and asked for the midpoint between the previous distance (5.5m at the 1.5m verge) and the current one (4m at the 0m verge) — putting the dogs' walk line at 4.75m. This is a logical setback for dog placement, not a return of the visual grass strip: the kit tiles pave 3–5m from the centerline, so in the kit-art path nothing visually changes and the earlier "no grass verge" decision (a visual call) stands — 4.75m sits within the paved band, near its outer edge. Only WorldBuilder's primitive graybox fallback renders the 0.75m verge as an actual grass strip.

A sidewalk's centerline sits RoadWidth / 2 + GrassVergeWidth + SidewalkWidth / 2 from the road's own centerline — 4.75m for the starting intersection's two roads. Road and Sidewalk (Core, Assets/Scripts/Core/World/) express this purely as that formula over WorldDimensions; a guard test (WorldDimensionsGuardTests) fails the build if any of the locked values is ever re-declared as a literal outside WorldDimensions.cs.

docs.title: Road arm extent
docs.text:
Each of the starting intersection's two roads (and, keying off the same extent, each road's two sidewalks) runs a fixed distance either way from the origin — NeighborhoodLayout.StreetHalfLength. That extent is half a tile (WorldDimensions.TileSize / 2 = 30m), so every arm reaches the tile edge. The WalkNetwork sidewalk arms and everything else derive from NeighborhoodLayout.Roads, so lengthening the arms extends the walkable sidewalks with them.

Decision (2026-07-31, Derek, on #392): the road arms extend the full distance to the tile edge. Previously StreetHalfLength was a hand-picked 26m — 4m short of the tile edge — so once the #147 backyard fences traced the lot quadrants nearly to the tile edge, a green band showed between each road arm's end and the edge, and on expansion two adjacent tiles' arms would leave an ~8m green gap instead of a continuous street. StreetHalfLength is now derived from WorldDimensions.TileSize / 2 (30m) — the same tile-edge convention the generic multi-tile system already uses (TileGeometry.EdgeMidpoint, LotBounds.QuadrantBounds) — so adjacent tiles' roads meet edge-to-edge and read as one connected street network. In the kit-art path, the visual road corridor tiles each arm with a whole number of City Kit road pieces compressed evenly to span exactly from the intersection tile's edge (5m) to the tile edge (30m) — the same compress-to-fit technique as the front-walkway pavers (#128, WalkwayTiling.PiecesAlong), scaling only the along-road axis so the road-band width and texture don't distort and no untiled sliver is left at the edge.

docs.title: The crosswalk box
docs.text:
At the starting intersection, the two crossing roads produce four box corners (one per compass direction the roads' sidewalks meet). Each of the 4 road arms — N, S, E, W — gets one crosswalk, CrosswalkWidth (3m) wide, connecting the two box corners on either side of that arm and letting a pedestrian cross straight over that road instead of going the long way around through both corners. A three-way (Tee) intersection gets one crosswalk per real arm — three, not four — with no crosswalk over its closed (roadless) edge.

Crosswalk rendering is derived per tile from the tile catalog geometry (TileCrosswalkGeometry.RectanglesFor, #508) — one patch per road-bearing edge of every intersection tile — so every unlocked intersection paints correct crosswalks, not just the hardcoded origin. (Before #508, both the kit crossing-tile placement and the primitive fallback read only the static origin NeighborhoodLayout.WalkNetwork, so an unlocked Tee rendered no crosswalks at all.) Only true crossings carry crosswalks: the 4-way and the four Tees. A straight, turn, or cul-de-sac tile has no crossing to paint.

In the shipping kit-art path, literal zebra-stripe crosswalks are baked into the Kenney City Kit Roads intersection mesh placed at the tile centre — road-crossroad-path for a 4-way, road-intersection-path for a Tee (its stripes on the three roaded arms only). WorldBuilder places the single mesh matching the tile's TileType, yawed per RoadTileArt (see Tile Catalog), so no separate crossing tiles are needed. Only WorldBuilder's primitive graybox fallback (when the kit tiles can't load) renders each crosswalk as a flat, distinctly colored rectangular patch with no markings, one per arm derived from the same per-tile geometry — see Art & UI Style for the fallback palette and Build checklist below for what's actually implemented.

A crosswalk is also a right-of-way point: a vehicle and a dog never occupy the same point on it, resolved by first-come yielding rather than driving through (#546). The claim is keyed on the crosswalk's WalkEdge (Core RoadCrossingGate), so it is per crosswalk segment and generalizes across every unlocked intersection and every current/future vehicle. A yielding vehicle stops far enough back that its whole body stays off the band — the stop is measured at its front bumper, not its centre (#639) — and it holds the claim until its tail, not its centre, has cleared the far edge (#658), so the 3m painted band is never shared at either end of the crossing. Those setbacks in turn bound how long a vehicle may be: an intersection's two bands sit 2 × (RoadWidth/2 + GrassVergeWidth + SidewalkWidth/2) = 9.5m apart, leaving a 6.5m clear gap between them, and a vehicle whose setbacks don't fit in that gap holds both crosswalks at once — which lets two oncoming vehicles deadlock (#660). See Dog Behavior § Yielding at road crossings for the full rule.

Visually, each crosswalk only covers the road and verge band — RoadWidth + 2 × GrassVergeWidth (7.5m at the 0.75m verge) — never the sidewalks themselves, which keep their own sidewalk-colored surface right up to the crosswalk's edge. The walk network's Crosswalk edge is still a straight line from one sidewalk's center to the other's (that's the real distance a dog covers crossing the road, and it's what keeps the graph connected to the sidewalk arm nodes) — this is purely a rendering clip in WorldBuilder, not a change to the graph.

docs.title: The walk network graph
docs.text:
WalkNetwork (Core) is a generic, data-driven graph over nodes (points) and edges — sidewalk segments, crosswalks, and front walkways — built from whatever Roads and house lots are passed to WalkNetwork.BuildFrom. The Roads are now derived from the live multi-tile map (MapWalkNetwork.RoadsFrom(TileMap), #398): every road-bearing tile in GameState.Map (the #109 grid) contributes its road segments from the Tile Catalog, so the graph spans every unlocked tile, not just the starting intersection. Per axis, a tile carrying a road on both of that axis's edges emits one full road through the tile centre (a FourWay emits both, exactly reproducing NeighborhoodLayout.Roads); a tile carrying a road on only one edge (a cul-de-sac / turn / tee stem) emits a half-length stub from the tile centre out to that edge.

Decision (2026-08-05, Derek, on #581): the walk network now curves at plain Turn* bends and cul-de-sac bulb turnarounds to follow the rounded road art, superseding this page's earlier "the rendered curve of a turn or cul-de-sac is independent of the graph edge" framing for those two cases. A playtest (v0.11) found dogs cutting a straight chord across a bend instead of following the curve. The fix inserts arc waypoints into the graph (see Curved corners below). Explicitly still straight: FourWay/Tee box-corner intersection turns stay hard 90° (their crosswalk box is unchanged) — only mid-tile road bends and cul-de-sac turnarounds curve. (The OpposingTurnsNS/OpposingTurnsEW twin bends were left out of scope here and then removed from the catalog entirely by #583.)

Decision (2026-07-14, Derek, on #128): the neighborhood has no driveways — front walkways replaced the DrivewayStub edges (WalkEdgeKind.FrontWalkway; the enum member was renamed, not duplicated) as each lot's connection to the sidewalk. A walkway runs from the house's actual front door — the #125 catalog door position at the #127 front-setback house position — perpendicular to the street onto the sidewalk, so dogs path to real front doors. It keeps the stub's two contracts: general wander never enters it, and it is the only way on/off a lot. The lot-side node of the connection is therefore the door, not the lot center; house lot centers (±14) remain as data anchoring the deferred expansion geometry, but no walk-network edge touches them anymore.

Construction, generically:

  1. Sidewalk arms. Every road's two sidewalks are split into arms wherever another road crosses them, so a sidewalk never runs through another road's own footprint. At a plain Turn* bend the two arms are clipped back RoadBendCornerRadius from the shared corner, where the curved arc takes over (step 4).
  2. Crosswalks. At each real crossing, the four box-corner nodes are connected pairwise into the 4-crosswalk box described above. A Turn* bend is not a real crossing — it emits no crosswalk box (see step 4).
  3. Front walkways. Each house lot gets one walkway edge from its front door to its street-facing sidewalk.
  4. Curved corners (#581). MapWalkNetwork.RoadsFrom emits a plain Turn* tile's bend as two independent perpendicular stub Roads meeting only at their shared tile-centre endpoint. WalkNetwork.BuildFrom distinguishes such a bend (the crossing sits at the end of both stubs) from a real crossing (interior to at least one road, e.g. a FourWay/Tee) and, instead of the straight box-corner connection, inserts arc waypoints along two quarter-circle arcs concentric with the road's own corner arc — inner (RoadBendCornerRadius − sidewalk offset) and outer (+ offset) — so FindPath traces the curve. A cul-de-sac's bulb turnaround is curved the same way: its two sidewalk arm ends are joined by an arc of radius CulDeSacBulbRadius (9m) bulging around the closed bulb. Each inserted arc is subdivided finely enough to read as a smooth curve regardless of radius (#598): the waypoint count is bounded by both a max angular step and a max world-space chord length (SidewalkWidth, 2m), so no single hop exceeds that chord. A fixed angular step alone was radius-blind — the large-radius 9m bulb got only ~3 long (~3.3m) chords and read as an angular octagon (a v0.11 playtest finding, follow-up to #581); the chord-length cap forces the big arc into many short hops so the polyline hugs the true curve. Because a dead-end bulb can't be told from a road running to the map frontier by road geometry alone, MapWalkNetwork passes the cul-de-sac turnarounds (one per single-road-edge tile) to WalkNetwork.BuildFrom explicitly, where the tile type is known; bends are detected geometrically from the roads. The inserted arc endpoints are the existing arm nodes, so the graph stays fully connected. The sidewalk edge nearest the lot center still decides which street the house faces (unchanged from the stub, and still what HousePlacement.FrontFacing keys off); from that facing, WalkNetwork.BuildFrom derives the house's front-setback position (HousePlacement's pure helpers) and its catalog door (HouseModel.FrontDoorWorldPosition), then projects the door perpendicularly onto that sidewalk (clamped to the segment) — splitting the sidewalk edge at the attach point if needed. The per-lot edge is queryable via WalkNetwork.TryGetFrontWalkway(houseId) (A = door node, B = sidewalk attach).

GameState.WalkNetwork is the live network dogs actually wander (#398): it is built (lazily, then cached) from the whole unlocked Map plus the lots of every built house, and rebuilt whenever the map or houses change — after a successful TryUnlockNextZone() or TryBuildHouse() (and on save-restore). A lot joins the graph (grows a front walkway) once its house has a resolved model to derive the door from — either an authored HouseStyleTable style (#64) or a zone-built house's rolled HouseVariant (#299/#414). Since #430 that includes zone-built houses: a built zone house gets a real front-walkway edge, so it renders and faces the street like a starting house. A freshly unlocked, house-less zone lot still has no House entry, so it stays off the graph (its tile's sidewalks/crosswalks still span it, since those derive from the map's roads, not its houses) — which also avoids the catalog throw a house-less lot would otherwise cause. The resulting network is fully connected across every unlocked tile — every node can reach every other node, including onto a newly unlocked cul-de-sac — which Core tests assert directly (BFS reachability). NeighborhoodLayout.WalkNetwork still exists as the bare starting-intersection network, used by Core tests that want it in isolation and as WanderBehavior's parameterless-network default.

WalkNetwork.FindPath is a small Dijkstra shortest-path over the graph (a priority-queue implementation would be overkill for a graph this size) — used by both wander and walking-home.

docs.title: Wander: a node-to-node walk over the network
docs.text:
WanderBehavior (Dog Behavior) no longer does centerline-bounce math on the streets directly. It now random-walks node to node over the sidewalk+crosswalk portion of the network. A front walkway is a wander candidate only for its own resident dog (#430): WanderBehavior carries the wandering dog's own HouseId, and a FrontWalkway edge is offered only when its owning house (looked up via WalkNetwork.TryGetFrontWalkway) is that dog's own house — so a dog may step onto its own front walkway, but every other dog keeps excluding all front walkways exactly as before. General wander therefore never detours onto a neighbor's lot, yard, or door. (A dog with no resident house — the NoResidentHouseId default — excludes every front walkway, the pre-#430 behavior.) A resident dog that has walked all the way up to its own front door returns back down the same walkway to the sidewalk (#517, generalized in #597): the door is the walkway's lot-side endpoint, a walkway-only node the general walkable set excludes, so WanderBehavior.NextTarget resolves a resident dog on the lot (door) side of its own walkway directly to that door node (via TryGetFrontWalkway) rather than through NearestWalkableNode — whose sole candidate edge is the walkway back to the attach point. "On the lot side" is detected geometrically against the walkway segment — the dog's projection onto the attach→door line is on the door-side half (up to a small overshoot past the door) and within the walkway's own lateral footprint — so it fires for a dog at, a hair short of, or just past the door node, while that narrow lateral bound stops any distant sidewalk node (which can be straight-line closer to a door than that door's own attach point) from ever triggering it. #517 matched only the door node exactly; because a dog stops a hair short of or just past the node, that exact match missed and the dog cut diagonally across the lawn to a sidewalk point off to the side (the #597 regression). Without any of this the door node's straight-line-nearest walkable node is a sidewalk point across the yard, and the dog cut diagonally across its own yard to reach it instead of retracing the walkway. Dogs actually entering the house or passing through to the backyard stays out of scope — a possible later follow-up. The walk is over the whole unlocked map (#398), so once a zone is unlocked dogs explore its sidewalks and crosswalks too, not just the starting intersection. A WanderBehavior (and DogView) binds to a live network provider (() => state.WalkNetwork) resolved on every hop, so an already-spawned dog picks up newly unlocked tiles the moment the map-derived network grows — no re-spawn.

At each node, the choice between continuing straight and deviating/turning is weighted. Two overloads exist: WanderBehavior.NextTarget(current, continueWeight, deviateWeight) takes an explicit override, while the parameterless WanderBehavior.NextTarget(current) — what every caller (DogView) uses today — derives continueWeight = 1 - TurnProbability and deviateWeight = TurnProbability from the dog's own MovementProfile.TurnProbability (#89). A lower TurnProbability (Excited) means a higher continue-weight, i.e. longer straight stretches before a turn, so the per-personality distinction from Dog Behavior carries all the way through to wander's actual path shape — both Speed and turn pacing now differ for Excited dogs, not just Speed.

docs.title: Ground height: sidewalks sit above the road
docs.text:
Related: #151

The Kenney City Kit Roads tiles model the sidewalk band raised a little above the road surface (a real curb, not just a color change) — placing a dog at a single fixed world-Y clipped its legs into that raised mesh whenever it stood on a sidewalk. WorldDimensions now locks RoadSurfaceHeight (0m, the road/crosswalk plane) and SidewalkSurfaceHeight (0.2m, measured directly from the shared kit road tile mesh) alongside the other world dimensions. WalkNetwork.GroundHeight (from, to) resolves which of the two applies to a hop between two adjacent network nodes from the specific edge connecting them — a Sidewalk or FrontWalkway edge resolves to the sidewalk height, a Crosswalk edge to the road height — rather than from either endpoint node alone, since a box-corner node (where a crosswalk meets its sidewalks) carries edges of both kinds and only the edge actually being crossed disambiguates them. DogView's wander step and DogSpawner's sidewalk spawn point both consume this Core query instead of hardcoding Y. A companion WalkNetwork.SurfaceHeightAt(point) answers the same road-vs-sidewalk question for a single arbitrary point rather than a graph hop — it returns SidewalkSurfaceHeight when the point falls on a Sidewalk or FrontWalkway edge's paved-band footprint (within half that edge's width of the segment) and RoadSurfaceHeight everywhere else (flat road lane, crosswalk, grass). The lost-item finder ring consumes it so the ring sits on the surface the hidden item actually rests on: on the kit's raised curb+sidewalk band it was previously fixed at the flat ground plane and rendered buried under that raised mesh, so on-road items showed no indicator (#580).

docs.title: Walking home routes over the network
docs.text: Walking home after accepting a "buy me X" quest (Quest Content) used to move in a straight line, ignoring streets entirely. Core now computes the actual route with WalkNetwork.FindPath from the dog's current position to its house's front door, ending via that lot's front walkway (#128 — the dog arrives at the actual door, which also feeds future quest arrivals); the Unity layer (QuestDirector) only consumes the returned waypoint list and walks it frame by frame (Vector3.MoveTowards hop to hop) — the Core/Unity split stays intact, per Testing Strategy. Dogs also spawn at their walkway's sidewalk attach point (DogSpawner), staggered along the sidewalk so housemates don't overlap.

docs.title: Walkway visuals
docs.text: A front walkway renders as tiled Kenney City Kit Suburban path-short pieces — the clean square-paver look, matching the kit sidewalk aesthetic (the kit's stone variants remain an available re-pick for Derek and Lucas). The math lives in Core (WalkwayTiling): pieces scale ×10 in width — the same derivation as WorldBuilder.RoadTileScale, landing the paver's 0.2 model width exactly on SidewalkWidth (2m), which is also the walkway edge's declared width — and along the walkway a whole number of pieces is compressed to cover door → sidewalk exactly (no gap at the door, no overshoot onto the kit road tile's raised sidewalk band). WorldBuilder instantiates the pieces verbatim, and falls back to one flat graybox strip when the kit piece can't be loaded — the same primitive-fallback pattern as the roads and houses. The world-build loop delegates to a per-lot WorldBuilder.BuildWalkway(lot) helper (#405) so a house built mid-game on a zone lot can render its walkway on the same code path; a lot with no front-walkway edge in the network it reads renders nothing, exactly as the loop skips it.

docs.title: Explicitly out of scope here
docs.text: • Approach-to-rest movement (#112) — RestBehavior stays a pure probabilistic state flip with no movement of its own; it doesn't touch the walk network. (Literal crosswalk striping is no longer deferred — it ships in the kit-art path via the baked-crosswalk intersection meshes: road-crossroad-path for a 4-way and road-intersection-path for a Tee, see The crosswalk box above.)

docs.title: Build checklist
docs.text:
• [x] Every road declares a sidewalk on both sides, set back 0.75m from the road edge (2026-07-13 midpoint decision — a logical setback for dog placement, no visual grass strip in the kit-art path), sized from WorldDimensions only
  • [x] The 4-crosswalk box exists at the starting intersection, one crosswalk per road arm
  • [x] Crosswalks derive per tile from the tile catalog geometry (TileCrosswalkGeometry), so every unlocked intersection paints them — a 4-way's four arms and a three-way (Tee)'s three, with none over a Tee's closed edge; non-intersection tiles get none (#508)
  • [x] Kit-art path renders the baked-crosswalk intersection mesh at each intersection tile's centre (road-crossroad-path 4-way / road-intersection-path Tee), yawed per RoadTileArt, instead of composing straights + separate crossing tiles (#508)
  • [x] Every tile type has a kit render path — each either resolves a RoadTileArt centre mesh or is a plain-straight type that tiles road-straight arms, guarded by MapLoaderTests.Load_RealAuthoredMap_EveryTileHasKitRenderPath. (This was a known limitation while the un-renderable OpposingTurns "twin bends" existed: #516 got them off the live map, and #583 removed the types from the catalog entirely — see Tile Catalog.)
  • [x] The walk network graph (sidewalks + crosswalks + front walkways) is generated from the roads and house lots, and is fully connected
  • [x] Plain Turn* bends and cul-de-sac bulb turnarounds curve — arc waypoints follow the road art (RoadBendCornerRadius / CulDeSacBulbRadius) instead of a straight box-corner chord — while FourWay/Tee box corners stay hard 90° (#581). Each arc is subdivided by both a max angular step and a max world-space chord (SidewalkWidth), so a large-radius arc (the 9m bulb) reads as a smooth curve rather than an angular octagon (#598)
  • [x] The walk network derives its roads from the live multi-tile Map (MapWalkNetwork), so it spans every unlocked tile; GameState.WalkNetwork rebuilds on zone unlock / house build, and dogs (bound to a live provider) wander onto newly unlocked tiles without re-spawning (#398)
  • [x] Each front walkway runs from the house's catalog door position to its street-facing sidewalk, perpendicular to the street (#128)
  • [x] WanderBehavior only ever produces positions on the sidewalk/crosswalk network — never a road surface, never a front walkway
  • [x] WanderBehavior's node choice supports weighted continue-vs-deviate decisions, defaulting to a per-personality split derived from MovementProfile.TurnProbability (#89)
  • [x] Walking home paths over the sidewalk/crosswalk/front-walkway network to the destination house's front door
  • [x] Front walkways render as tiled City Kit Suburban path pieces along the Core segment, with a graybox strip fallback when the assets are absent (#128)
  • [x] WorldBuilder renders road, verge, sidewalk, and crosswalk as visually distinct placeholder-colored surfaces in the primitive fallback (the kit tiles bring their own art); spawned dogs stand on sidewalks
  • [x] Crosswalks render only over the road itself, never over sidewalk pavement
  • [x] Dogs standing or walking on a sidewalk rest at the sidewalk's raised surface height, not the road's — WalkNetwork.GroundHeight resolves the right one per edge (#151)
  • [ ] On-device visual check (human task, not attempted here)

docs.title: Tile Catalog (Design Reference)
docs.text:
Related: #105 (this page), #106 (sidewalks and the walk network, implemented — see Sidewalks & Walk Network), #109 (multi-tile grid/placement system, implemented), #86 (map-shape question, resolved 2026-07-14 — see Neighborhood Expansion)

Status: implemented in Core (#109)

The catalog, grid-coordinate tile map, placement/adjacency validation, and per-type property-lot definitions are built in Doggiehood.Core.World: TileType (16 values — the 15 road tiles plus the roadless GreenSpace added by #539; the two OpposingTurns "twin bends" were removed outright by #583), TileTypeDefinition/TileCatalog (road edges), TileCoordinate/TileMap (placement + adjacency), TileGeometry (world-space derivation), and TileLotCatalog (per-type lot slots for the 15 lot-bearing types — every type except the roadless GreenSpace). The starting FourWay intersection still uses its own hand-placed NeighborhoodLayout rather than this generic system — but its road arms now reach the tile edge (NeighborhoodLayout.StreetHalfLength = WorldDimensions.TileSize / 2 = 30m, no longer the old hand-picked 26m), so when expansion places a neighbouring tile the two tiles' road arms meet edge-to-edge and the street network reads as continuous (#392; the kit-art corridor compresses a whole number of road tiles to fit each arm exactly, à la WalkwayTiling — see Sidewalks & Walk Network). Zone unlock/house-building on top of this geometry (v0.4's #55/#56/#57) is still future work — this issue only builds the geometry itself; procedural tile selection stays explicitly out of scope, per Neighborhood Expansion. Sidewalks, crosswalks, and the walk network graph are implemented separately (#106) — see Sidewalks & Walk Network — using a generic, data-driven graph rather than this tile/adjacency system.

docs.title: Standard dimensions
docs.text:
These measurements are locked in Core (WorldDimensions, #105; the road-bend corner radius added by #581) as the geometric basis every tile type below will eventually be built from.

Standard Value Tile size 60m x 60m Road width 6m Grass verge (road edge -> sidewalk) 0.75m — Derek's 2026-07-13 midpoint decision (in conversation; originally 1.5m, briefly 0m the same day): a logical setback that puts the dogs' walk line at 4.75m from the road centerline, within the City Kit road tiles' paved band (#121/#122); no visual grass strip in the kit-art path — see Sidewalks & Walk Network Sidewalk width 2m Crosswalk width 3m Cul-de-sac bulb radius 9m Road-bend corner radius 5m — the plain Turn*/road-bend road centerline's corner-arc radius, measured from the shared road-bend kit FBX (raw radius 50 at the raw×0.1 world scale, midline of the inner 20-raw and outer 80-raw asphalt-edge arcs). The walk network curves a bend's sidewalks concentrically about it (#581); see Sidewalks & Walk Network

docs.title: Grid coordinates
docs.text:
The world is an integer tile grid addressed as (x, y) — x runs east/west, y runs north/south. In Core these map to TileCoordinate.Col (x) and TileCoordinate.Row (y); world-space is derived by TileGeometry (Col → +X, Row → +Z). The starting FourWay intersection is the origin (0, 0); the tile directly north of it is (0, 1), directly east is (1, 0).

A tile's identity is its integer (x, y); a type name's compass suffix (e.g. CulDeSacEast) describes which edge carries the road, not where the tile sits on the map. Position comes from the coordinate, connectivity from the type/code below — keeping the two separate avoids the "is that northwest or is that an east-facing cul-de-sac?" confusion.

docs.title: The 15 tile types
docs.text:
Each tile is a 60m x 60m square with roads entering/exiting along some subset of its N/S/E/W edges. FourWay is the existing starting tile (#7, #38); the next 14 are built for the multi-tile grid (#109). A 16th roadless GreenSpace tile (#539) is listed at the end of the table below and detailed in its own subsection. Two further OpposingTurns "twin bend" types were part of this catalog until #583 removed them — see Removed: the opposing-turn twin bends.

The Code column is the compact authoring token (see Tile codes below); it encodes the same road edges as the "Road edges" column.

Type Code Road edges Sketch FourWay NSEW. N,S,E,W ╋ — the starting tile StraightNS NS--. N,S ┃ StraightEW --EW. E,W ━ TurnNE N-E-. N,E ┗ TurnNW N--W. N,W ┛ TurnSE -SE-. S,E ┏ TurnSW -S-W. S,W ┓ TeeNorth N-EW. E,W,N ┻ (east/west with north half only — upside-down T) TeeSouth -SEW. E,W,S ┳ (east/west with south half only — T) TeeEast NSE-. N,S,E ┣ (north/south with east only) TeeWest NS-W. N,S,W ┫ (north/south with west only) CulDeSacNorth N---. N ╹ road enters from the north edge, ends in a bulb CulDeSacSouth -S--. S ╻ CulDeSacEast --E-. E ╺ CulDeSacWest ---W. W ╸ GreenSpace ----. (none) ▦ a roadless full-tile park/open-grass tile — see Green-space tile below

docs.title: Green-space tile (#539)
docs.text:
GreenSpace is the 16th type: a full grid tile the same size and shape as the other 15, but carrying no road on any edge (empty RoadEdges) and no buildable lot (TileLotCatalog.LotsFor(GreenSpace) = zero lots — no houses, ever). It is authored into the target map (docs/tools/map-data.json) exactly like any other type — {x, y, type: "GreenSpace"} — and its empty road-edge set means it validates through TileMap.CanPlace only against neighbours whose shared edge is also roadless.

Distinct from unbuilt-quadrant green space (the open-grass fill inside a placed road tile, described under Property lots per tile — a static property of a tile's own type). This GreenSpace tile type turns an entire tile on, and unlike the paid, road-connected expansion frontier it auto-activates for free — no coin cost, no lock icon — the moment 2+ of its 4 edges border an already-activated tile (a placed road tile or an already-activated green space), cascading unbounded to a fixpoint.
